en: The regulations for the monastic community (*sōrin*) have already been detailed by the Great Wise Chan Master Baizhang.

However, as the times grew distant, later generations sought convenience and eventually fell into habitual practice. Although there may be differences across various regions, they have never deviated from its fundamental principles.
During my time living in the assembly, I frequently saw my peers transcribing the *Conglin Ruyong Qinggui* (The Pure Regulations for Daily Use in the Monastic Community).

These various versions contained mutual omissions and discrepancies. Later, during a period of leisure, I consulted all available manuscripts to reconcile their differences while preserving their commonalities.

I transcribed them by hand with great care, resulting in a work that is remarkably detailed and complete. I have titled it *Conglin Jiaoding Qinggui Zongyao* (Essentials of the Revised Rules of Purity for the Forest of Monasteries) and divided it into two volumes, upper and lower, so as to facilitate reading.
The possession of these *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity) for our school is like the possession of the *Li* (Rites) for the Confucian tradition.
The Sūtras state that ritual follows what is appropriate and adapts through increase or decrease according to the times; this is why the present work was composed following the Great Wisdom [Sūtra].
All of these matters were researched and recorded by successive generations of senior virtuous predecessors.

Out of ignorance, I have not dared to privately alter them—by adding or subtracting—as previously described. Rather, I have examined their differences, preserved their commonalities, and brought them into harmony.

So it is. May those who observe this not take offense. Written on the second day before the commencement of the retreat in the tenth year of the Xiachun era, the Jiashu year, by the Bhikṣu Weimian at Jiwankuan (Studio for Contemplative Play) by the Back Lake.

The Special Envoy requests the Abbot; the Abbot accepts the request.

As for the invitation of the Abbot: the temple’s *kūsō* (storehouse office) shall convene the *chiji*, *shushō*, those in private quarters, and the *kōgu* (venerable elders) to offer tea and determine the date.
First, a *gyōja* (attendant) or *rōrō* (senior official) is dispatched to deliver the letter; the stationery is provided by the *kūsō*.

The *katō* (guest master) delivers it to the quarters of the *shushō*, where they further deliberate and appoint one of the two classes of officials—or someone from among the later ranks—to serve as the special envoy (*senshi*).
The Hall Master, or the Secretary, or a senior monk from a single quarters (*dānlǐo*), or the Abbot himself, shall serve as the host.

The Kitchen Office shall provide tea and refreshments for the reception. The Abbot, together with the special envoy, shall proceed ahead. The Manager of Affairs and the Treasurer shall prepare the account books;
should any matters arise during the journey, they shall consult with the special envoy. On the day of departure, the Monastery Gate shall offer tea at the entrance.

The attendant (táng) performs the ritual duties on behalf of the guest, as would a special envoy. Upon arriving at the temple, if one is invited to take up residence for the current term, one should first visit the Guest Prefect (zhīkè), followed by the Administrative Office (kūsī).

Once settled in one's quarters, one prepares a formal letter of introduction (ménzhuàng) and first visits the Head Monks (tóushǒu), then the individual monks' cells (dānliao)—though no letter is required for these latter visits.
When these formal greetings are concluded, one then arranges the written invitations (shūtiè) in the dormitory hall and requests the Abbot (zhùzhí rén) to come forth.

[The guest] and [the host] look at one another. Incense is burned, and they perform prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*kṣauma*). They present their inquiries and submit the formal documents (*śū* and *tiè*).

Next, the Guest Master (*zhīkè*) leads them to pay respects at the various quarters and the administrative offices (*xíngtáng*). (In some places, they first enter the Abbot’s quarters (*fāngwǎng*), announce their arrival, and briefly present their inquiries; only then do they attend to the formal greetings at the various locations.

On the following day, the arrangements are set, and the administrators (*zhīshì*), head officers (*tóushǒu*), and senior elders (*qíjiù*) are invited to the Hall of Rest (*qìntáng*) to examine the documents. The Hall Office (*tángsī*) assembles the community to offer congratulations. This applies when inviting the West Hall Officer, head officers, or senior elders from another monastery.

The special envoy enters the gate and first sees the guest prefect (*kṣāṇavārika*). He is led to the Abbot’s quarters (*upādhyāya*) for formal greetings. The Abbot escorts him to his assigned lodging.

Next, he proceeds to the administrative office (*kośa*) and the various monastic quarters (*lao*) to perform the customary greetings. Once these formalities are completed, he returns with the attendant to the Abbot’s quarters to report:

"At such-and-such a temple, we have now invited such-and-such a person. He then goes to that person's quarters to report the matter, after which he performs the formal greetings, burns incense, and performs the full prostrations (*mahāpraṇāma*).
Three prostrations. Present the memorial and the invitation letter. On the following day, invite the abbot of the temple to join the two classes of officials in making the formal request.

Upon reaching the third request, once it has been accepted, determine the date on which the invitation will be received. The special envoy must spend the night apart from the temple and inform the abbot, burning incense and paying respects, saying:
"I respectfully request the Master to come tomorrow to serve as the presiding master for the newly appointed monk. On that day, arrange the memorial and the invitation letter within the Dharma Hall.
The drums were beaten to assemble the congregation. The special envoy, together with the attendant, requested the abbot to emerge and ascend the seat to preach the Dharma.

As for the newly appointed elder, he was simply requested by the special envoy himself. (Songyuan [Xuedou] led the assembly while concealing his room; he did not engage in formal questioning. Xianyan led the assembly for Songyuan, likewise without questioning.

Shiqiao led the assembly for Master Ji, engaging in questioning. Xianan led the assembly for Fuan, also engaging in questioning. There are many such differences among the various masters’ traditions. If one is a newly ordained person who is a dharma heir, they shall reside at that temple.

The junior monk shall hold the seat. The Dharma robe should then be conferred. (The special envoy should also prepare one robe for the new person. The new Elder takes up the robe; there is a formal discourse.
Having donned the robe, he proceeds to the foot of the Dharma seat. He requests the host to spread out the mat and performs nine full prostrations to express gratitude for receiving the Dharma.

Thereafter, he takes up the memorial (shu-tie). If it is not the case of a "Dharma-son" (a successor), he simply takes up the robe immediately after the abbot has descended from the seat (if the robe has not yet been taken up, he takes up the memorial first;
each occasion has its own formal discourse). The special envoy receives it and passes it to the rector (wei-na) and others. Once it has been read aloud, he points toward the Dharma-seat.

(For the *yǒufǎyǔ* [Dharma-discourse] ceremony: Ascend the seat. First, offer incense and offer prayers for the Emperor. Next, the officials (if there is occasion, offer the incense of dharma-succession; or, if it is an entry into the monastery, offer it at that time).

Next, solicit a topic for discourse, engage in question and answer, present the outline of the teaching, express thanks, and conclude the session. (If this is a dharma-heir, he descends from the seat and performs three prostrations with full body contact before the abbot to thank him for serving as witness. If he is not a dharma-heir, [he does not do so].)

Descend from the seat and proceed with the customary greetings (*renshi*). First, offer greetings to the Abbot. *Words of thanks:* "In a lifetime of service, I have sought only to fulfill my duties; I look up with shame at the sages of old. Since your three invitations were so earnest, it is difficult to refuse your compassionate command.

I am overwhelmed by a sense of awe and trepidation. *Words of congratulation:* "The needle in the bag has already been revealed; the falling flowers cannot conceal it. It is fortunate that you have accepted this post; I humbly pray for your joy and celebration. Next, offer greetings to the administrators (*zhishi*), the heads of departments (*tou-shou*), and the assembly.

*Words of thanks:* "I have received this appointment by mere grace, which brings me to shame before the tradition of our school. I am deeply indebted to your support and encouragement; I cannot contain my gratitude. *Words of congratulation:* "Rejoicing in the invitation of devas and humans, you add glory to the light of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. My humble sentiments..."

I am filled with the utmost joy beyond measure. The Abbot, together with the two classes of officials, shall escort [the new abbot] to his quarters. The Guest Master and Attendant shall lead him on a tour of the monastic cells (as is done for those of former standing in the *mengtang* hall of this temple;

whether he is escorted upon receiving the official notice is at their discretion, or may be omitted. However, if he is currently holding office or resides in a private cell, it is proper to escort him through the public areas; whether he accepts or declines is not restricted. In some places, once the invitation has been accepted and the formal greetings concluded, he is escorted immediately).
When the special messenger arrives at the time of the meal, the meal for the invited guest is prepared, and the new abbot is arranged within the Sangha Hall.

He sits facing the Abbot (if inviting the incumbent, the seating arrangement is not required). The special envoy proceeds in person, lighting incense and making the formal invitation according to the usual protocol.
For the other quarters, the guest master of the temple shall go with the special envoy and attendant to invite those in the various lodgings.
Once the notice boards have been posted, at the time of the meal, the special envoy waits before the front gate of the Sangha Hall for the Abbot and the new Elder.
Entering the hall, they bow and take their seats. First, they inquire after the health of the abbot; next, they inquire before the newly appointed elder.

They proceed from behind the sacred image to the center of the hall to burn incense, then move to the upper and lower sections of the hall, exiting through the outer door; first the lower section, then the upper section.

Having finished arranging the incense burner, inquire after the abbot and the new ordinand once more. Next, inquire after those inside and outside the hall, as well as those in the upper and lower sections.
Enter the center of the hall and inquire after them there. Exit the hall and eat. Next, burn incense and offer the monetary gift (*dakṣiṇā*); first, for the abbot.
Next, the new arrivals; next, the assembly of monks. When the meal is finished, they take their seats to drink tea. The special messenger enters the hall and burns incense before the Sacred Monk.

Having burned incense inside and outside the hall as previously described, he first pays his respects before the Abbot, then pays his respects before the new arrivals, and finally returns to the center of the hall to stand and pay his respects.
Once the tea has been served to everyone and the soup pitcher has been removed, the Abbot’s cup is collected first.

Offering a cup to the new resident: The special messenger proceeds directly before the new resident, performs two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full bows, and escorts the new resident out through the rear gate.
Next, he proceeds before the abbot, performs two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full bows, and escorts the abbot out through the front gate.

Upon reaching outside the gate, he performs a greeting by bowing with his hands lowered; then he re-enters the hall, burns one stick of incense, performs two prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths and three full bows, and circumambulates the hall once.

Upon reaching the outer hall, one returns to the center of the hall to perform a greeting (*wensun*). The bowls of the assembly are collected, the drum is struck three times, and the seats are withdrawn.

(If the incumbent is being invited, one performs the rites before the Abbot; the beginning and end are the same. Next, the special envoy shall go to the administrative office (*kusī*) to thank them for preparing the meal.

It is also appropriate to go to the Abbot’s quarters and to the place of the new appointee to offer thanks, saying: "I was not fit to trouble Your Reverence just now, yet I am humbly grateful that you have [condescended to]... [The new appointee follows].

One should first consult with the special envoy regarding the abbot’s invitation to the seat (*yinsuo*), the presentation of offerings (*zhikai*), the person who will proclaim the memorial (*shu*), the senior monks (*qijiu*), the two classes of officials (*liangban*), and fellow countrymen from the past.
Offerings should be distributed among them so that the ceremonies are properly observed; one must not go to excess in seeking reputation or wasting the monastery’s permanent assets (*changzhu*).
After the meal, the new arrivals should visit each of the quarters (*liao*) in turn to pay their respects. That evening, the special envoy...

Invite the newlyweds and the host. At the evening bell, serve soup and fruit. Then invite the administrative officers (*jishi*) and heads of departments (*tou-shou*) to accompany them. The newly appointed officials shall prepare the reception for the new arrivals;
the monastery administration (*shanmen*) shall specially provide soup and fruit. The two classes of officials and the great elders (*daqijiu*) shall also accompany them.
The following morning, tea is served. A separate meal is prepared to entertain the new appointee. This is requested by the attendant in charge of guests;

the special envoy is requested by the head of the guest office. There is a monetary gift (*kṣaṇa*) provided. Furthermore, the administrative officers (*karmadāna*), heads of departments, and senior elders are invited to accompany them.

The attendants of the special envoy are treated according to their respective ranks. On the day of departure, the new appointee and the special envoy go together to the Abbot’s quarters (*upādhyāya-śālā*) to pay their respects and take leave.

The various quarters also exchange formal leave-taking one night prior. If the head seat (śrāmaṇera) is to assume office elsewhere, there is a formal departure from the assembly with a lecture in the hall.
Prior to this, he instructs his own attendant or a special messenger to borrow the Dharma seat from the abbot’s quarters (vāra-mukha) in advance, though the Dharma cloth is not yet spread.

Once he has ascended the seat and descended, he first takes leave of the host, then the two classes of officials, and finally the great assembly. The administrative office (kū-si) prepares for the three gates.
The seats are arranged and tea and soup are prepared. The Abbot (Zhuchi) occupies the eastern seat; the Head Seat (Shouzuo) takes his place to the side;

and the newly appointed official occupies the southern seat. A special service is held, and senior elders (Dajiujiu) are invited to accompany them. The Administrative Head (Dusi) performs the rites, and the Great Bell is struck to see them off, manifesting the grand ceremonies of the Mountain Gate (the monastery).

If the Xitang or senior elders receive their appointment letters, the ceremonial protocols for departure may either be performed in full or omitted, depending on the circumstances. This is determined by the presiding authority.
The person [in charge] prepares the offerings. As the sedan chair is about to depart, the great bell is also struck to see them off.
If it is the incumbent abbot, on the day of departure, he shall ascend the hall to take leave of the assembly; beneath the Dharma seat, he shall bid farewell to the entire community together.

At the head of the three gates, tea and soup should be prepared, with a seat arranged facing south. The Head Seat (shouzuo) occupies the position of honor, while the West Hall (xitang) or a senior monk (daqi) is invited to sit there.
Old Ritual: Separating into Pairs and Sitting Opposite One Another. The two groups divide into east and west and sit facing each other. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) performs a bow and takes his seat.
He burns one incense stick before the Abbot and bows in greeting. Returning to his position, he serves the hot tonic.
Rising again, he burns another incense stick, advances before the Abbot to bow, and then steps back to burn a "companion incense" stick. He then bows in the center.

Upon returning to the designated station, tea is served; the cups are collected, and the guest is escorted onto the sedan chair. Whether the two classes of attendants escort the guest or are excused from doing so depends on the host’s discretion.
If there are accompanying followers, they should have returned to the temple in advance to be sent to their quarters; a note may be issued to the Hall Office (Tangsi) to send them there first.

Alternatively, if they enter the monastery with the host, they should follow the host on the tour of the halls. Nowadays, many people prefer to be sent back to the hall first, for the sake of convenience.
The task is accomplished; each may proceed as they see fit. If there are those who have shared quarters with him, they should be exempted from this.
26. Entering the Monastery as a New Abbot:
Whenever a new abbot enters the monastery, he should observe where he shall reside—whether with the two classes of officers (the *liangban*) or with the *xitang* and senior *qishi*.

The Former Resident: Upon arriving at the place of lodging, one should inquire after the health [of the abbot] (the temple administration may provide a palanquin). If the temple is located nearby, the entire assembly should go together to inquire.
The administrative officers (*jishi*) shall calculate the schedule in advance and inform the newly appointed attendant.
If the new abbot is occupied with affairs or has previously issued a written exemption, then the two classes of senior elders (*daqijiu*) should also go to inquire; this must be understood.

Regarding the time for the *shiqu* (the person taking charge) to enter the hall: on that evening, the attendant shall instruct the *xingzhe* (novices) to arrange the morning sequence one by one so that no confusion occurs at the last moment.
The Hall Superintendent shall have the *xingzhe* post the notice board (*guapai*) the night before to inform the assembly.
When the appointed time arrives, the ritual implements are struck. The assembly exits through the outer triple gate and stands in formation from the far end toward the near.

Upon reaching the entrance, they welcome the abbot. When the abbot reaches the entrance, he points to the triple gate (with a formal discourse). Next, he proceeds to the Buddha Hall to burn incense and prostrate (with a formal discourse). Next, he returns to the Sangha Hall to register his arrival.

According to the *Chanyuan Qinggui*, when a new abbot enters the triple gate, he does not untie his bundle; he points to the triple gate (with a formal discourse). Next, he returns to the guest quarters (*danguo*) to wash his feet. First...

Upon returning to the Sangha Hall to register one's stay, one then enters the Buddha Hall to burn incense. (In some cases, there are those who practice the ancient rites; this also follows the intention of the Abbot. Regarding the method of registration:

the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck, and the assembly first returns to their respective bowl-positions and stands in place. The Abbot burns incense before the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ), followed by his fellow practitioners.

Perform three prostrations with the sitting cloth fully spread out. The Rector (Vina) shall face him and inquire after his well-being. Then, he requests the Abbot to return to his bowl-position (pat-wei), whereupon he performs three prostrations with the sitting cloth touching the ground;

the Abbot replies with one prostration. (Note: At Shaolin, Zhulin, Jingci, and Lingyin, it is required that both classes of attendants escort the Abbot together back to the bowl-position, where he receives three prostrations with the sitting cloth touching the ground. Next, the Rector...
Lead the procession around the hall once. Facing the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ), stand side-by-side to inquire after his well-being and then exit. The attendants follow behind.

(According to the *Chingui*, the new abbot first enters the hall to burn incense, pays respects to the Holy Monk, and together with the attendants, performs three full prostrations (*dazhan sanbai*). Together they circumambulate the hall once. The Rector invites him to his bowl-seat, where he performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli sanbai*), and then hangs up his robe.

Next, proceed to the Hall of the Local Deity and the Patriarchs' Pagoda to burn incense. (Whether or not there is a formal dharma-verse depends on the abbot’s intention. Thereafter, enter the Abbot’s Quarters to burn incense.

A single stick of incense is lit. [The Abbot] takes his seat. After the attendant has performed the inquiry (monshin), the Master delivers his formal discourse (hōgo). When it is finished, the ritual assistant (gyōja) enters with the desk.
The Chief Administrator (tōji) steps forward to perform the inquiry and presents the temple seal. One should have prepared the desk, brush, inkstone, and the temple seal in advance.
The petition is then prepared and laid upon the table. The Abbot examines the seal; the Chief Administrator (Jūshi) opens the seal and presents it.
The Abbot first signs his name upon the petition, followed by the date. The attendant applies the seal over the date.

The petition is retained by the Chief Administrator, while the seal is immediately resealed and returned to the robe-and-bowl cabinet (ibatsu-kaku), where it is entrusted to the robe-and-bowl attendant. Alternatively...
The attendants follow the practitioner. When the practitioner steps back, the Abbot rises; the administrative officers (zhishi) and the entire assembly step forward and take their places.

The Chief Administrator (dutong) burns incense, then steps back to perform a mutual inquiry (wenshen). They perform two prostrations with palms opened and three full prostrations, then offer congratulations, saying:

"We humbly receive that the Venerable Master has graced this Dharma seat; our hearts are filled with boundless joy. The Abbot replies with thanks, saying: "I am ashamed of my own unworthiness, yet I have been honored by this illustrious monastery; our hearts are filled with boundless trepidation. The administrative officers then step back. The Head...

The head of the senior elders (shu-da-giju) steps forward to offer congratulations. The attendant in charge of guests (katō gyōja) calls out: "Please invite the West Hall [monks], the administrative officers (chiji), the heads (shu), and the senior elders to the dormitory hall for the serving of hot water.

After the hot water is finished, the monks from various mountains and visiting guests meet one another. When the tea and hot water service are concluded, there is a brief rest. The Chief Administrator (dutō) prepares a formal document to invite them to the midday meal.
Carrying incense, he proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to report the matter. The attendant of the storehouse office prepares boxes and cloths to carry the documents.

The Head of the Monastery burns incense and presents the documents according to the usual procedure. Next, he instructs an attendant to invite the abbots from various mountains, the West Hall, the administrative officers, the heads of departments, the senior elders, and the special envoys for tea and refreshments.
After they have rested briefly, the attendant who burns incense reports to the Abbot regarding the midday meal.
Before ascending the hall, the attendant is instructed to notify the administrative officers, the heads of quarters, and the various monastic residences to post their name-boards.
He is further ordered to have an attendant prepare incense tables and censers in advance on the eastern side of the Dharma seat. The special envoy shall burn incense and perform the rites;

the Abbot shall incense the memorial scrolls and documents, while simultaneously engaging with the visiting Zen guests for formal dialogues. The Chief Administrator (Dusi) is to request the Rector (Vinaya-master) in advance.

The Head Seat (Shouzuo) oversees the proclamation of the official documents (shu), placards (tie), and so forth. (First, the Imperial Edict (chihuang), the Provincial Decree (shengza), or the Prefectural Notice (futie) are read, followed by the monastery’s own petitions (shanmen shu) and the petitions from various monastic communities (zhushan shu), which are proclaimed in sequence. In some places, the Chief Administrator (Dusi) and the Head Seat do not proclaim them themselves;

instead, they assign subordinate personnel to do so. There is also a portion of the monetary offering [for these duties]. Prior to the midday meal, the attendant (xingzhe) first informs the Attendant (shizhe) and strikes the drum. Next, he informs the Abbot (zhuchi).

The Attendant must inquire about the arrangement of the documents before the Dharma Seat (fazuo) and the request for the Rector (weina) to proclaim them, and so on. [This concludes the] preliminary procedures.
Whether [the incense] is prepared or not, and how many pieces of incense are required for the offering, must be arranged the day before; furthermore, these matters should be confirmed at the time.
Only one piece of incense for the Dharma heir is to be taken from the abbot’s own breast and presented at the appropriate moment.

When the attendant waits for the abbot to emerge from the sleeping hall and take his seat, the attendant shall perform a formal greeting (monshin) directly in front of him and then move to stand on the eastern side. The abbot’s attendant (fangzhang xingzhe) shall likewise perform a formal greeting directly in front of him.
Having finished the questioning, he turns and stands at the western side. The attendant, however, descends from the Dharma Hall and stands at the northeastern corner.
At the second watch, the assembly gathers; the special envoy enters together with the attendant and requests the abbot to come forth.

For now, he stands to the left of the Dharma seat, facing south (as when one first enters the world, having received an invitation elsewhere: if there is a formal discourse upon picking up the robe, it shall not be repeated here; if no such discourse has been given, one should first pick up the robe and deliver the discourse, and only then don the robe).

The special envoy burns incense and receives the imperial decree (du-chi), the yellow edict (huang), or the provincial warrant (sheng-zha) and its accompanying notice (tie). Next, the abbot concludes the formal presentation of the memorial (shu).

The envoy personally receives each document one by one and hands them over to the attendant (xingzhe), who then passes them to the person designated to read them aloud. Furthermore, he has two attendants prepared in advance.

Carrying the memorial scrolls (shūtei), first consult with the attendants (shijō) to review them. When holding up the scrolls, if there are several sets of Dharma words (hōgo), and if each one has its own Dharma words, then pass them through one by one in sequence.
Retire to your position and wait until the recitation is finished. Then, burn incense again, perform two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full prostrations (sanpai).

Depending on the circumstances, the abbot (jūji) may waive this, or you may perform a touching bow (sokusurei), or a mere greeting (monjun); or, if it is the opening of the hall (kaidō), you shall offer prayers for the Emperor (shusei).
The officials first offer their own incense. Then, [the abbot] points toward the Dharma seat (and delivers a formal discourse). He ascends the seat;

first, he offers incense to pray for the Emperor, next for the officials, and next to clarify his Dharma lineage. He takes his place on the seat (as the attendant offers incense one by one, which must be received in an incense censer and inserted into the burner one by one).
If this is the opening of the hall, one representative from each of the various mountains, or the head monk, stands to the right of the Dharma seat and strikes the mallet, saying:

"The assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast should contemplate the primary truth. When the abbot utters these words and the Zen guests engage in dialogue, it is what is known as "opening the hall" (*kaidō*).

This has existed since ancient times; for instance, when receiving an invitation from the capital, it was customary for an official appointed by the imperial court to invite the master to a specific temple to perform the *kaidō* ceremony on behalf of the Emperor, with all expenses provided by the government.
Consequently, provincial governors and prefects followed this precedent, sometimes inviting the master to the provincial office or to the city hall.

Whether at a separate temple or at the original temple, all matters must be submitted by the official for approval. Expenses such as offerings and monetary gifts are likewise to be paid by the government.

It is improper for those entering the monastery today to arrogantly open the hall on their own authority. Once the question-and-answer session is concluded, the *tígāng* (summary of the discourse) is presented; when the *tígāng* is finished, the expressions of gratitude follow.
If there are officials, donors, or abbots from various mountains who have escorted the master into the monastery, the attendant must instruct the guest-master to inquire into these matters in detail.

Regarding the protocol for addressing [the officials]: address each person by their title, offering thanks one by one; there is no need for extensive conversation, as the purpose is solely to offer auspicious prayers for the Emperor.

If there are no officials present, or if they have departed together, thank the Special Envoy, the West Hall Abbot, the administrative officers (*zhishi*), the head administrators (*tou-shou*), and those in the single quarters and the infirmary (*mengtang*).

After the elders of the various quarters, the members of the great assembly, and those who have arrived for a brief visit have finished their expressions of thanks, the session is concluded as it was at the opening of the hall.

Again, the mallet is struck, saying: "Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma King. The abbot descends from his seat, first thanking the officials and escorting them back to their lodgings.

Returning to the Dharma Hall, they discuss matters of courtesy (*renshi*). If this is not a formal opening of the hall (*kaitang*), the special envoy steps forward to burn incense, performs two prostrations with the sleeves extended (*liangzhan*) and three full prostrations (*sanbai*), and offers words of thanks.

If the ceremony is waived, they perform a mere bow (*chuli*). The attendant instructs the acolyte to move the candle stands before the seat into a single-line formation (*yizishi*) and to advance the incense table.
The acolyte of the Hall Administration (*tangsi*) calls out for the exchange of courtesies, and the *Rector* (*weina*) inspects the list of participants.

Hand this down to your disciples so that there may be no errors. [The Master] shouts, "The affairs of the various mountain monasteries. Next, he shouts, "The affairs of the West Hall. Such are the varying degrees of ritual protocol.

While maintaining the *jūji* (abbot’s) posture, the following announcements are made: First, the announcement for the *chiji* (administrative officers) and their staff is made; the assembly performs two full prostrations with both hands extended. Next, the announcement for the *tōsu* (head monks) and the general assembly is made.

Next, the announcement for the senior monks (*daigikujō*) residing in single quarters is made. Next, the announcement for the *mongu* (monks of the meditation hall) is made. Next, the announcement for the senior monks of the various quarters is made—or alternatively, the announcement for the personnel of each individual quarter is made.

Next, the announcement for the *hōkan* (dharma relatives) is made. Next, the announcement for the local laypeople (*kōnin*) is made. Finally, the announcement for those who have arrived temporarily to offer congratulations is made.
Next, the various *xingzhe* (attendant practitioners) perform their prostrations. They must first enter and take their seats, then request the master to sit before they prostrate.

Next, the *cansui* (attendant-followers) and other *xingzhe* are invited to enter and perform their prostrations. Following this, the six *shiju* (corpse-removal) *xingzhe* perform their prostrations. Finally, the assembly of *chadou* (tea-head) *xingzhe* performs their prostrations.
Prior to the formal lecture (*shangtang*), the attendant instructs the *xingzhe* to hang the "Circuit of the Hall" plaque; the abbot then conducts the circuit.
The Quarters. Beginning from the first quarters on the eastern corridor, the residents of each quarters go outside to receive [the visiting monk] and escort him out.

In cases where there are many people in a quarters, only the head of the quarters (寮元) shall welcome and see off those entering and leaving; the rest of the community shall simply stand outside the gate.

When the Abbot returns to his quarters (方丈), the Chief Administrator (都寺) shall visit the quarters to invite him for a special tea ceremony following the midday meal. The Tea Notice: select a person to arrange it.

Virtue. [The name] is written upon silk. This rite is most solemn. If there is no plaque, one must submit a formal petition; the Abbot (Dusi) shall carry incense and perform prostrations according to the usual protocol.
Upon the conclusion of the meal, the assembly withdraws from the Second Hall to partake of special tea, which must be served before the meal.

The attendant (hakseong) is instructed to invite the heads of the community and the great assembly to accompany [the Abbot]. The illumination board is prepared and the head of the retreat (chamdu) is notified. Attendants are dispatched to serve the tea.
When the meal service in the administrative office (*kusi*) has concluded, the guest master (*katō*) attendant is instructed to wait for the abbot and then strike the drum to announce the assembly.

Once the head administrators (*tōsu*) and the assembly of chief officers (*shushō dajū*) have gathered and settled, the guest master receives the abbot outside the hall, escorts him back to his seat, and bows in greeting (*monjun*).

He then passes behind the sacred image (*shōsō*), proceeds to the center of the hall to bow, and stands for a short while. When the assembly has sat down, he burns a single stick of incense, joins his palms (*sashu*), and turns his body toward—
He bows before the *jūji* (abbot). Again, he passes behind the *shōsō* (holy monk) and stands bowing in the center. Tea is served to everyone.

When the tea-pitcher is brought out, the *tōji* (chief administrator) approaches the *jūji*, bows, and offers tea. He then turns back, passes behind the kitchen, and returns to stand bowing in the center.
First, he collects the *jūji*'s cup. Then, the entire assembly of administrative officers enters the hall; the *tōji* takes his place in the north row.
The Chief Administrator (Shou) performs two prostrations with fully extended hands before the Abbot.

The Administrative Head (Du Si) proceeds from north to south, turns to lead the assembly of administrative officers past the rear of the Holy Monk’s shrine, and exits the hall to stand at his position.

The Chief Administrator alone stands outside the hall in the lower section at the head of the wooden platform, awaiting the Abbot’s exit from the hall to offer a formal greeting. The Chief Administrator then re-enters the hall and burns one stick of incense.

The four head monks inquire after one another’s health. They collect the bowls of the assembly. The drum is struck three times, and they withdraw from their seats. The Abbot returns to the Treasury Office (Kūsi).
He prepares a chest and cloth cover again, and carrying incense in his sleeve, he goes to the Abbot’s quarters (Hōjō) to request that tonight in the Sangha Hall, a special soup-offering (tō) be held.

Furthermore, he instructs the attendants to invite the assembly to accompany him and to arrange the notification boards; he reports this to the Head of the Assembly (Santō) and orders the attendants to serve the soup. The soup...

The ritual is also like the tea ceremony. (If there is a tea notice board, it is first hung between the upper and lower sections of the Dharma Hall until the time for the special service arrives; it is then moved and hung between the upper and lower sections in front of the Sangha Hall. Prior to the serving of the hot water.
The attendant covers the small *can* (private discourse) and instructs the attendants (*xingzhe*) to notify all the quarters to post the notice board.
When the evening bell tolls, the attendants first inform the attendant and then the abbot. The drum is struck once and the assembly gathers.

The attendant invites the abbot to come forth. Generally, for a small *can* upon entering the monastery, this is equivalent to the day’s formal lecture hall session; it consists solely of expressing gratitude to the officials.

[The assembly] disperses. The patron, the various mountain monasteries, and the members of the host’s household have not yet been thanked; therefore, the administrators (*karmadāna*) and the special envoys are thanked for their diligent efforts in traveling from afar to carry the formal invitation and welcome [the guest].

Furthermore, the two classes of officials are urged to remain, as they may not yet speak of retiring. After the formal greeting is concluded, the attendant of the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) shouts:

“I request the West Hall Master, the administrators, the heads of departments, the elders of the single-dwelling quarters, the attendants, and the Zen guests to come to the abbot’s quarters for the serving of hot tonic. Fruit is also prepared.
The *zi* (disciple) and the attendant burn incense; after consuming the medicinal broth (*tang*) and completing the inquiries (*wensun*), they descend together with the *zi*.

The attendant performs an inquiry before the abbot and then returns to his seat to sit (in all instances of being granted a seat, follow this procedure). The following morning, after the gruel meal, he again invites the West Hall Master, the two classes of officers, and the senior elders to the Abbot’s quarters for tea.
As at Gongde Temple: on the following day, after the morning gruel has been finished, one should act as the patron (dānapati) and ascend the seat to offer incense and offer prayers.

Having descended from the seat, one gathers the assembly and proceeds to the ancestral hall (*sìtáng*) to chant the scriptures. Alternatively, if this is done on the day of entering the monastery, the offering of incense is performed together with that occasion.

On the subsequent day, one simply employs the ritual of offering incense and flowers to gather the assembly for the chanting of scriptures. Nowadays, whenever one observes the day of entering the monastery, [the practice is] to proceed to the ancestral hall to offer incense first, and then...

On that day, the Abbot shall specifically ascend the seat to recite the sutras. After entering the monastery and completing the formal audiences with officials and donors, he shall specially bestow *dakṣiṇā* (offerings) upon the special envoy and his entourage, as well as those who drafted the announcement placards (*bǎngshū*).
Following established precedent, he shall also provide offerings for the robe and bowl cabinet and for the placards;

if the placards were commissioned from a separate scribe, they too shall receive offerings according to custom. Finally, he shall entertain the two classes of officials and the senior elders (*dàqǐjiù*).
While in attendance, when you have a brief moment of leisure, you should invite the senior and junior elders for tea and inquire about precedents and past practices.

You must verify the assets of the mountain gate, such as imperial calligraphies, official edicts, land deeds, and precious vessels, and ensure that the monks in charge of these items are properly appointed.
Examine the ledgers one by one to ensure they are clear and transparent.
Fearing that those who disregard cause and effect may commit fraud during the exchange of monastery assets, this is established so that future generations may investigate such matters.
If it is an imperial appointment, one must wait for the special envoy to arrive carrying the imperial edict. As soon as they reach the temple, one should immediately express gratitude.

A table for incense, a censer, and a candle stand are arranged before the Buddha Hall, facing north. An additional table is set up to hold the imperial edict. The bell is struck to assemble the community.
The abbot faces north toward the palace, offers incense, and bows his head while speaking in a low voice: "The current Emperor, His Majesty..."

"Ten-thousand-year reign! Ten-thousand-year reign! Ten-thousand-times-ten-thousand-year reign! This humble monk [Name], respectfully receiving the Imperial Edict to serve as the Abbot of [Name] Temple—this humble monk [Name] is deeply moved by the Imperial Grace. His lower emotions are beyond words; he gazes toward Heaven and looks toward the Sage with the utmost urgency and trepidation.

When the assembly disperses, the Abbot returns and receives congratulations in due order. On the day of entering the monastery, prior to ascending the seat, he shall again offer thanks for the Imperial Grace according to the previous protocol.
Once the new abbot has entered the monastery, he should first pay his respects at Gongde Temple;

next, he should visit the local prefectures and counties, as well as the lay patrons residing nearby and the various monasteries. He must examine each of their formal letters of introduction (*menshàng*) with great care.
If there is a message from a patron residing nearby, he should personally go to visit them with courtesy. This is because when one possesses a temple, one must rely on external support.
Guardianship. Gold and grain are maintained in perpetuity and disbursed daily; one should merely follow established precedent and must not abruptly introduce new practices.

For now, entrust these matters to the two classes of officials, each performing their respective duties. Regarding vacancies in the communal quarters (*zhòngliáo*) or the quarters of the heads (*tóushǒu*), the treasury office (*kùsī*) should be authorized to provide what is required.
When there is no clamor from either the inner or outer circles, the atmosphere will naturally become harmonious. Now, as for those who act as masters...
Noble! Treat others with generosity; approach affairs with solemnity. Examine the orthodoxy or heterodoxy of speech; recognize the confusion and delusion of arrogance.

One must not fail to show compassion for those who toil and suffer; one should likewise take responsibility for one’s own faults and transgressions. If you can act in this manner, then your vessel will be large and its resonance profound;

when the root is flourishing, the branches will naturally thrive. In antiquity, monasteries were established for the sake of the elderly and the infirm; such was the purpose for which they were ordained.

The Hall Master shall administer medicines and tonics, while the administrative office shall ensure that the monastic estate provides sufficient supplies for these needs; this is the regulation established by the Buddhas of the past.
Furthermore, among the eight fields of merit, the direct care of the sick is ranked first. Yet nowadays, in various regions, the "Longevity Halls" exist in name only and lack substance.

When a patch-robed monk encounters illness, it is like being imprisoned; this is truly pitiable. Should there be no one from his local community to look after him, the public authorities ought to dispatch someone to attend to him, so that he may recover as soon as possible.
It is the custom at Tiantong that for every sick monk, a small servant is assigned to provide for his needs.
As those who serve as abbots, you should extend the compassionate heart of a Bodhisattva and pay careful attention to this matter.

Furthermore, when there are those who are nearly elderly seeking to join the community as resident monks, one should not obstruct them. One who can carry out these two matters is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Regarding the matter of construction and maintenance, one must not diminish the resources of the community to initiate new projects or alter established regulations simply because one thinks, "I am the abbot;
I can accomplish this. Nor should one sit idly by while things fall into ruin day by day; rather, one should manage the permanent endowments (*sāṃghika*) accordingly.
Whether through the presence or absence [of the master], one should guide and transform others toward the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), bestowing benefit upon future generations.

If the mountain gate occasionally dispatches representatives to the four quarters—whether as monks or as itinerant practitioners—they should be provided with a successor. Furthermore, events such as the establishment of assemblies must never be neglected; one should reflect on the difficulty with which the ancients established these traditions.
When a donor arrives at the mountain, they should be received with earnest hospitality, so that faith may be further expanded.
27. The Procedure for the Entrance and Exit of the Two Classes of Monastics (Appendix:

The Entrance and Exit of Attendants and the Invitation of Renowned Virtuous Head Seat Holders) On the day following the Buddha’s birthday, the two classes of monastics are invited. That evening, when the dusk bell tolls, the former administrative officers proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to announce their departure.
They offer incense and perform a prostration with full body contact (*chuli*). Among them, if there are those whom the Abbot wishes to retain, he shall light a lamp and escort them back.
The Kusi (Storehouse Office) serves hot soup. The Attendant follows the Abbot to the Kusi, where they burn a single stick of incense and serve the soup;

no one from the various quarters remains behind, and thus there is no formal escorting. Early the next morning, after the "Universal Rice Porridge" gong has been struck in the Hall, the administrators enter through the rear gate.

The Chief Administrator strikes the gong once and says: "I inform the assembly: Yesterday, we received the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, the Venerable Master, ordering us to enter the Kusi to serve as administrators. We have now come..."

When the mind grows weary, announce one’s departure and return to the hall. (Having respectfully announced this,) strike the mallet once more. From behind the shrine of the Sacred Monk, pass to the left and proceed directly before the Abbot.

Perform two prostrations with hands fully extended (*liǎnzhǎn*) and three full prostrations (*sānbǎi*). Having completed this, turn around and pass behind the kitchen of the Sacred Monk to the right, emerging before the Sacred Monk to perform three full prostrations with hands fully extended.
Turn around to pay respects to the Abbot, then turn again to inquire after the first head monk at the head of the row.

[The Abbot] stands. The practitioner strikes the bell, collects the bowls of the assembly, and strikes the drum three times; they then exit the hall. The ritual for the conclusion of the summer retreat (*kṣayana*) is identical to that of the winter year.
On the fourth day of the month, the Abbot specially prepares tea for the assembly. He prepares a chest and a double-layered box, along with an incense burner and an incense case.

Before the midday meal, the guest-inviting attendant goes to the Head Seat’s quarters to inquire after his well-being and burn incense, performing one prostration with the body touching the ground (*chuli*), saying:

"Venerable Abbot, you have invited the Head Seat to attend a special tea ceremony in the Cloud Hall following the midday meal, as a mark of respect for this particular occasion. The guest master shall be instructed to post a notice from the abbot at the front of the Sangha Hall; this notice shall be posted on the eastern board.

The notice for this shall be posted on the western board in front of the Sangha Hall. Next, one shall proceed to the Abbot’s Quarters (Fangzhang) and the various other quarters to extend the invitation, all according to the same protocol as the soup service.

The Head Seat (Shouzuo) specifically prepares tea for the subordinate head officials (xiàshǒu tóushou). He also goes to their quarters to invite them, using a box and cloth cover (xiāngfù) and presenting a formal petition (zhuàng), following the same ritual as before.

The petition is also posted on the lower section of the wooden boards in front of the Sangha Hall. Furthermore, he goes to the Abbot’s Quarters (Fāngwǎng) to offer incense and pay his respects while making the invitation.
As is the usual custom, the Abbot’s quarters and the administrative office (kūsī) use a formal notice (bǎng), while the Head Seat (shouzuo) uses a written petition (zhuàng).

If the Head Seat is newly appointed, he shall also serve as the assistant head official; tea shall be specially prepared for him, and the procedures for his invitation and reception are identical to those previously described.

Tea is served in the hall for three days. At the time of the midday meal, the long board (the "long board" refers to that which is struck three times in a long roll after the fire drum, not the three strikes following the wooden fish;

nowadays in monastic communities, the three strikes of the board are generally treated as the "long board," and the formal rite is performed accordingly—this may simply be adjusted according to the occasion. Before the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ-saṃgha), burn one stick of incense, perform three full prostrations, fold up the sitting mat (niṣīdana), rise to inquire after his well-being, and proceed to the head of the first row.

Facing north, perform a deep inquiry after his well-being, circumambulate the hall once, and exit through the outer hall. First descend the lower section, then the upper section, and return before the Sacred Monk to inquire after his well-being and withdraw;

this is called "Requesting Tea" (qing cha). [The Chief Seat (śrāmaṇera) and the Administrative Head (karmadāna) use these same rites; before the Abbot (sthavira), the inquiry after his well-being is performed...]

After the formal inquiry, one proceeds from the head of the platform to inquire after the entire hall. Following the midday meal, the *zhào-pái* (attendance board) is arranged outside the Sangha Hall.
If the Abbot specifically invites the Head Seat and the assembly, the administrative officers (*zhīshì*) shall accompany them. The Head Seat and the Abbot face each other;

the Administrative Head (*dūsuì*) stands on one side of the Abbot, the Deputy Administrative Head (*jiànsì*) stands on the other side of the Head Seat, and the other administrative officers follow in order behind the Administrative Head and the Deputy Administrative Head.
When the drum signals the start of the meal, the attendant waits in front of the hall for the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) to arrive and receives his greeting.
Once the Head Seat enters the hall and stands at his bowl-position, the attendant follows behind him to offer a greeting and requests him to leave his position.

The Head Seat walks ahead, while the attendant bows and invites the head officials and senior monks to follow. They proceed directly to the place specially prepared for the Head Seat, where they offer their greetings. From here...
Behind the niche of the Holy Monk (Śrāmaṇera), the attendant exits through the right side of the hall to receive the Abbot. The *xingzhě* strikes the bell seven times. The Abbot returns to his seat.
The attendant stands in the center to perform a greeting (*wènxùn*). The assembly each takes their seats. (The Head Seat and the Chief Administrator receive the Abbot as he returns to his seat;

they should perform a greeting and bow him into his seat, then pass behind the kitchen area to the center to perform a greeting before the assembly finally takes their seats. The attendant offers incense with the left hand before the Holy Monk, followed by offerings at the upper and lower sections.
Having finished burning incense outside the hall, enter the hall and place the incense casket with its lid closed back in its original position.
With palms joined, proceed directly to the head seat (shouzuo) to perform a greeting. Passing behind the kitchen, exit on the right side and go straight to the first seat at the head of the row.
Facing north, perform a deep greeting. Circumambulate the hall once; upon reaching the chief administrator (dutong), turn slightly and perform a greeting. Then, exit the hall.

First, go down to the lower section; next, go up to the upper section, circling through until you have traversed the entire hall. Enter the center of the hall, perform a greeting, and stand. Serve tea throughout the hall.
When the soup pitcher has been removed, join your palms together. Go once more before the Head Seat (shouzuo), perform a greeting, and again pass behind the kitchen area, exiting from the right side.

Perform a greeting in the center, prostrate three full prostrations with the sitting cloth fully spread, and fold the sitting cloth. Circumambulate the hall one circuit as before, return to your position and stand. This concludes the duties of the attendant (xingzhe).
First, collect the special cups for individuals and the abbot’s cup. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) comes forward before the abbot to express gratitude for the tea.

He performs two prostrations with the sleeves spread and three full prostrations (for each spread of the sleeves, the abbot returns one bow; because this is a matter of great importance for the assembly, when the Head Seat performs three prostrations by touching the ground, the abbot returns only one bow—though there are some abbots who simply waive this and do not return even one bow).

For the first spread of the sleeves, he presents the words of thanks, saying: "I humbly receive the honor of the Venerable Master’s preparation of this tea; my humble heart is filled with boundless gratitude. For the second spread, he inquires after the abbot’s health.

The Announcer says: "Today [at this specific time of the season], we respectfully wish that the Reverend Abbot’s health and daily life be filled with myriad blessings. Then, one performs three prostrations with the forehead touching the ground (*chuli*).

In the interim, burn incense sticks as companions; after offering a greeting, withdraw. (In some places, one also offers greetings in both the upper and lower sections. The practitioner collects the bowls, and the drum is struck three times.
Only then does the abbot emerge from the hall again. The assembly descends from their seats, and the head seat (shouzuo) immediately proceeds to the abbot’s quarters to thank him for the tea.
Usually, when the abbot reaches the Dharma Hall and awaits the arrival of the head seat, he dismisses the courtesy, and the head seat simply offers a greeting and withdraws.
The *dutou* specifically invites the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and the assembly to take their seats and perform the rites, all of which are identical to the previous procedure.

However, having finished burning and placing the incense in the censer, he proceeds directly to the front of the Head Seat to bow; thereafter, he turns behind the shrine of the Sacred Monk (*shengseng*).
He proceeds directly before the abbot and performs a greeting. Only then does he turn his body to face north and perform another greeting. He then patrols the hall.

When the tea has been served to all and the tea pitcher has been removed, he goes again before the person for whom the service is specifically intended and performs a greeting. Rising as before, he performs a greeting before the abbot. Having finished the patrol of the hall, he first collects the offerings for the abbot and the person for whom the service is intended.

The person holding the tea cup and the head temple administrator (Dusi) lead the assembly to the abbot’s presence. "On this day of coarse tea, we humbly receive the Honored Abbot’s compassionate descent upon us. We are moved beyond measure by your kindness. After another prostration with opened sitting cloths, they say:

"In accordance with the current season, we respectfully wish that the Reverend Abbot’s health and daily life be ever blessed. Upon reaching the prostration with touching foreheads (chuli), the abbot returns three prostrations, and the administrators turn around.
Passing behind the kitchen, they exit the hall and line up at the head of the beds in the lower section. Standing in the morning posture, they wait for the abbot to emerge and perform a greeting.

When the long board (changban) sounds, the guest-inviting attendant (qingke shizhe) shall go around the hall to invite the guests to perform the rites, which are identical to those for the "untying of knots" (jiejie).

However, after the meal, once the incense-burning attendant (shaoxiang shizhe) has bowed and returned to his position, and after the incense burning in the center of the hall as well as inside and outside the hall is completed, he shall place the incense censer back in its original location. With palms joined (chashou), he proceeds directly before the head seat to pay his respects (wensun).

[The attendant] emerges from the right side of the Honored Sangha, stands at his position to perform a greeting, and distributes tea to everyone. When the vessel has been passed out, he joins his palms and proceeds again before the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) to perform a greeting.
He returns to his original position, performs a greeting, and stands there. First, he collects the cups for the Abbot and the Head Seat.

The Head Seat goes before the Abbot, performs two full prostrations with hands extended, and the Abbot returns the bow. Once the Abbot has finished returning the bow, the Head Seat [returns] from the Honored Sangha.
Passing behind the monks' niches, exit through the right side of the hall. The abbot follows behind and escorts him out, where he exchanges greetings with the Head Seat (shouzuo).

The abbot re-enters the hall and takes his seat; the attendant burns one stick of "accompanying incense" in the center and performs a greeting (in some places, the upper and lower sections also perform greetings).

Only then are the bowls of the assembly collected, the drum is struck three times, and the session concludes (performing two prostrations with both hands extended and three bows; there are also those who discuss the matter of "high [status]"). Generally, [the procedure for] the front...

During the two *zhǎn* (prostrations), the abbot does not return the bow; rather, with both hands, he makes a gesture of parting. This is because the other intends to perform a prostration, and the abbot avoids it with his hands. Thus, the other withdraws. When the other performs another *zhǎn*, the abbot again avoids it, and thus the other performs a *chùbài* (a touching bow).
At that point, the abbot should also perform a *chùbài* in response. (This is seen in detail in the *Shìshì yàolǎn*).
30. Special Small-Seat Soup Ceremony:
Generally, prior to the recitations during the seasonal festivals, the Abbot strikes the drum for the Small-Seat Soup ceremony, which is divided into three sessions. First Session.
For the second session, the drum is struck again specifically for the accompaniment of the West Hall Chief Seat (Xitáng Shǒuzuò).

For the third session, the drum is struck again specifically for the accompaniment of those currently serving as administrative officers (zhíshì), heads of departments (tóushǒu), those in single quarters (dānlíáo), senior elders (dà qǐjiù), and the West Hall.

For the fourth session, the drum is struck again specifically for the accompaniment of those who have previously served this temple, as well as those from various regions who have been prominent figures and have experienced service in this monastery, including those of high renown in the Rear Hall (Hòutáng).
Accompanying [the guests] to their seats, they sit separately. The seating cards are arranged and three sets of tables are prepared;

furthermore, name cards for the first, second, and third seats are placed so that they are easily visible, ensuring that no confusion occurs at the time of the service. The attendant must personally supervise this.

The two attendants who burn incense and invite the guests shall perform the same formalities together, such as bowing to invite them to sit and offering the medicinal broth (*yōu*). However, if it is a special occasion...

The ritual for this is as follows: next, perform the recitation; next, strike the drum; serve the hot water for the great seat in the Sangha Hall; and the Chief Administrator (Jūji) performs the rites. Thirty-one:
On the fifth day of the fourth month, a special tea ceremony is held specifically for newly ordained monks before their first summer retreat.
After the incense offering has concluded, a special tea is served by the Abbot at the time of the midday meal. On the following day, the administrative office (Kositsu) proceeds to...

On the day following the special tea service for the Kūtang (Treasury Hall), the various *dǒushǒu* (head officials) arrange a special tea service in the Zhàotáng (Illumination Hall). Seating is prepared in the *chén* (courtyard) area.

The *fāngzhàng* (abbot) and the *kètóu* (guest master) attendants inform the *shìzhě* (attendant official), who then prepares a seating list according to the *jièlà* (seniority by ordination age) tablets.

Then, invite the newly arrived monks to sign their slips; each shall write beneath their name, "So-and-so respectfully obeys your command.

If it is a slip for a Head Official (tóushǒu) or the administrative office (kùsī), once the name has been written, one may either write the character "know" (zhī) or the two characters "obeys command" (zūnmìng); this depends on the person's preference.

If there are individuals from various regions who have registered at the outer quarters (*wai-liao*), they must be instructed to have an attendant carry their registration forms (*dan-zi*) to request signatures.

Once the signature has been obtained, the form from the Abbot’s quarters (*fang-wang*) shall be presented to the Attendant (*shi-zhe*); the form from the Kitchen Administration (*ku-si*) shall be presented to the Kitchen Administration; and the form from the Head Officials (*tou-shou*) shall be presented to the Head Officials.
Each form shall be verified point by point, and the administrative attendants shall be ordered to arrange the cups and saucers and prepare the hot water flasks.
Preparation: Set up the name-boards (*zhào-pái*) according to seniority in ordination (*jiè-là*). Place the name-boards on the western side of the Dharma Hall (*fǎ-táng*).

Those from the Five Mountains (*wǔ-shān*) and other eminent figures from various quarters shall be assigned to the head seats and subsequent positions; the Head Seat (*shǒu-zuò*) shall accompany them.

When the meal is concluded, the attendant (*xíng-zhě*) informs the Attendant-in-Chief (*shì-zhě*), who then informs the Abbot (*fāng-chāng*). The drum is struck, and the Attendant-in-Chief waits for those who have newly registered at the western side of the Dharma Hall.
Assemble. Bow and enter. After exchanging greetings with the abbot, take your positions according to the seating chart and stand still.

The two attendants for burning incense and inviting guests shall move to both sides and bow to the assembly as they circulate through their stations (it is sufficient to bow once while circulating the entire group; it is not necessary to bow at each individual station). Once the assembly is nearly seated, the attendant for burning incense steps forward, offers one stick of incense, and turns toward the east.
The guest-inviting attendant proceeds before the foremost person on the western side;

they simultaneously exchange greetings face-to-face with each of them, turn to join their palms, and proceed in order until the final seat, where they briefly exchange greetings and then stand with hands folded, starting from the head of the row.

Circumambulate and inquire after [the master's] well-being as before. Having completed the circumambulation, return to the center and stand firm. Serve tea to everyone; the tea pitcher is brought out. On both sides, proceed as before.

Circumambulate and inquire after [the master's] well-being. Once the invitation to drink tea is finished, the incense-burning attendant steps forward again to burn one stick of "accompanying" incense (*xiāngbànxiāng*).

Stepping back, he performs an inquiry together with the assembly. The cups are collected, the drum is struck three times, and the newly arrived head of the assembly, together with the rest of the group, steps forward.

First, offer thanks for the tea. Perform two prostrations with the hands extended and three bows, or perform the *chuli* (touching the ground), or simply exchange greetings, according to the discretion of the presiding official (*zhuchi*).
When the meal concludes, the *zhishi* (administrative officer) strikes the wooden board and stands at the presiding seat by the illuminated plaque, awaiting the arrival of all new guests.
They bow and enter. Each returns to their respective position and stands. The various *jishi* (administrative officers) stand in the center and wait for the assembly to settle.

The *jishi* then divide to both sides and bow as they circulate through the rows to invite everyone to be seated. Once the circuit is complete, they all return together to the master’s seat and sit briefly. The assembly withdraws their feet and then rises in unison.

They burn incense—either burning it all at once in a single burner or burning it separately in three burners. Once the incense caskets have been placed in their respective positions, they divide into two groups.
At the edge of the platform, he bows facing the assembly. Turning around, he proceeds to the final seat at the end of the row, where he likewise bows facing the assembly.
He then returns to the center and stands in formation. One person from the upper hand advances again to burn a single stick of incense for the accompanying spirits.
They withdraw and bow together, then all return to their seats to drink tea. The ceremonial protocol for the head officers from beginning to end is identical.

The Abbot holds tea service in the Abbot’s Quarters (fangzhang), the Dharma Hall (fatang), or the Meditation Hall (shuiantang). The administrative officers (zhishi) hold it in the Storehouse Hall (kutang), and the Head Monks (toushou) in the Brightness Hall (zhaotang).

The Chief Seat (shouzuo) and the Administrative Head (dusi) go together to the Abbot’s Quarters to borrow the tea seats and the tea drum. Once the Abbot’s tea service is concluded, the drum is struck again.
The head administrators (shoushi) act as host and guest to one another, each performing the prostrations twice. Each strikes the drum and withdraws from their seat.

At the conclusion of each tea service, the newly arrived representative (chantou), together with the assembly, rises and steps forward to express thanks for the tea. He makes the gesture of unfolding his sitting mat (zuoju), but the host shall waive this formality.

after the midday meal, the head of the quarters writes a formal request to invite the entire community to perform a special rite for the purpose of "untying the knots."

Regarding the serving of hot water (*tāng*): set up the signboard as usual and request the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader), the various attendants, and the *kṣetrajña* (Guest Master) and bath master to accompany you.

33. The Head of the Community Quarters (Śrāmaṇera-śālā). Regarding the Head of the Community Quarters serving tea during the summer retreat:

On the day after the morning gruel has been finished, the tea attendant (caḍu) is instructed to invite the Head of the Quarters (Lao-yuan) and the Master of the Quarters (Lao-zhu), and to post the notice board.
The Head of the Quarters and the Master of the Quarters sit separately before the Avalokiteśvara image. The person serving the tea prepares [the implements].
Situated inside the quarters door on the upper hand, facing the head of the quarters (shōnin). Upon the conclusion of the meal, the attendant strikes the board in front of the quarters.
The tea server first goes outside the quarters door on the lower hand, stands with palms joined, and bows for the assembly to enter. Once they have finished entering, [the attendant]...
Incense is burned in three censers. Turning to the front of the central censer, one first bows to the *liàoyuán* (head of the quarters).
Next, turning to the rear, one bows to the *liàozhǔ* (master of the quarters). Then, turning again before the upper and lower censers, one bows once more.

Returning to the center, one stands and bows. The *liàoyuán* rises and gestures for the tea server to be seated. When the tea has been consumed, the tea server rises and returns to the space between the central and lower areas.

Standing with hands joined. The Chief of the Quarters (Liaoyuan) goes before the incense burner to thank [the abbot] for the tea, escorts him out, rises, bows three times before the burner, and then returns to the center to bow to the Chief of the Quarters.

[The guest] sits. When the tea is finished, he rises and stands before the incense burner to exchange greetings with the *diànzuò* (steward), saying: "Today we have received this coarse tea; it is a great honor that you have condescended to visit. The *diànzuò* replies:

He inquires after [the master’s] health face-to-face, joins his palms, and exits from the eastern side. He likewise first lifts his left foot and, having stepped outside the door but within the matting area, performs a prostration by touching the ground and then withdraws.

Daily sitting meditation after the dismissal of the formal meal. The attendant of the Hall Office shall first notify the Head Seat following the morning gruel, and then strike the board in front of the various quarters.

The assembly returns to the hall and takes their seats. Next, the secondary head (fu) and the subsequent heads return to the hall. Once things have settled slightly, the head seat (shouzuo) is notified again.

Once everyone is seated (if one wishes to relieve oneself, it is only at this time that one may rise), when it is nearly time for the release from meditation (*fangchan*), the attendant of the Hall Office (*tangsi xingzhe*) shall wait in attendance and report slowly and calmly to the Abbot.
Next, he reports to the Head Seat (*shouzuo*). From behind the Holy Monk’s kitchen, he turns to the right, exits to the front of the hall, and briefly shakes the board below [the plaque].

Upon this, the Abbot, the Head Seat, and the various heads of the community shall rise, and the assembly may then attend to their own convenience. Although the bell is not struck after the meal, [the procedure remains as described].
[The above] is the formal rule. However, those who practice the Way do not restrict themselves by this. When the evening bell tolls, they enter the hall to practice *zazen*.
The Head Seat (Shuso) enters the hall to burn incense and circumambulates the hall once when the second session bell is about to end, then returns to his position.
The Abbot enters the hall to burn incense and circumambulates the hall once when the third session bell is about to cease, then sits down; it is only then that the bell tolls.
