The Śūraṅgama leader then chants, "At that time, the World-Honored One... and so forth, and recites the mantra. Upon finishing the chanting, he calls out, "Mahā! The rector then performs the dedication once more, saying: "The above sutra chanting..."

Dedicate these merits toward the *tathatā-bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), adorning the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit. May the four debts of gratitude be repaid and the three realms of existence be equally sustained; may all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu* together perfect the *sarvajñajñāna* (all-encompassing wisdom). [As for] the "ten directions and three periods of time," and so forth—[if this is recited], the assembly does not prostrate.

On the following day, which is the head of the *Śūraṅgama* [recitation], one performs the dedication, saying: "The aforementioned present... and so forth. When encountering the new or full moon, it is the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) who performs the dedication to pray for the longevity of the Emperor.
Alternatively, every day after the morning gruel, when descending from the hall, one should immediately chant the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. Thus...

It is not necessary to go to the Scripture Library Hall to chant the sutras. As on daily occasions after the morning gruel, when the board is struck again, one chants the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* assembly and then descends from the hall.
One still uses the Scripture Library Hall to chant sutras and offer prayers for the Emperor. The concluding distribution is the same as the rites for the opening ceremony;

however, once the chanting of the dhāraṇī is finished, the head of the *Śūraṅgama* assembly chants, "This is the Buddha’s *Uṣṇīṣa-prabhāsa-rāśi*... and so forth, and finally calls out "Mahā! three times.
That dedication is as stated in the opening invocation; then they disperse.

Nine: After the meal, the attendants (xingzhe) of the Land Deity Hall and the Recitation Hall post the notification board for the assembly. Before the morning session, they go to the Land Deity Hall to pay respects to the Patriarchs.
In the Hall and the Great Buddha Hall, the incense is prepared and the candles lit; the preparations being complete, the report is made to the Abbot and the two classes of officials.

Everything follows the sequence for the three-eighth-day recitation. The administrative officers (zhishi) pre-emptively burn incense and prepare tea and soup. When the board sounds, the assembly gathers.
The Abbot exits the Buddha Hall, strikes the board in front of the Kitchen Hall three times, and immediately the great bell is struck. The Abbot arrives, burns incense, and withdraws. The *weina*...
He steps forward from the assembly, bows to the abbot to offer incense, and next bows to the two classes of officials to offer incense. Turning around, he pays his respects to the abbot;

when this sequence is complete, the *vinaya-dhara* turns and recites before the local deity (the text for which appears below). He then performs the dedication, saying: "By the merit of the recitations above..."

I dedicate this merit to the local deities of this mountain and the presiding spirits of this hall. It is my hope that your divine radiance will provide harmonious support, manifesting deeds of beneficial brilliance so that this Buddhist garden may flourish preeminently and forever bestow impartial blessings. (Once again, I beseech the venerable assembly to turn their thoughts toward the ten directions and the three periods of time...)

The Summer Retreat begins. It is said: As the warm breeze fans the wilds and the God of Fire presides over the quarter, this is the time when the Dharma King observes the *pāda-bandhana* (foot-binding retreat), and the day when the Śākya sons protect living beings.
We reverently assemble the great assembly and solemnly proceed to the sacred shrine to recite and uphold the vast and majestic names of the Ten Thousand Virtues.
I dedicate this merit to the true masters of this hall. May they grant their protection so that our request for a peaceful retreat may be fulfilled.
We rely upon the Great Assembly to recite: "The Pure Dharma Body... and so forth.

The Summer Retreat is Concluded. It is said: When the golden wind fans the wilds and the White Emperor presides over the quarter, it is the time when the Buddha, the King of Awakening, releases the retreat regulations. This is...
On this day, as the Dharma-year comes to its full completion, the ninety-day retreat has passed without hindrance and the entire assembly has remained in peace.
We recite and uphold the vast and auspicious names of the myriad virtues to look up and repay the true lords of this hall. We rely upon the mindfulness of the great assembly... [and so forth].

Winter Solstice. We reflect that as the season approaches the end of the year and the festival arrives when the clouds are recorded, it is the moment when the first yang returns and the beginning from which the myriad species are born.
We reverently assemble the great assembly and solemnly proceed to the sacred shrine to recite and uphold the vast name of the Ten Thousand Virtues.
Dedicate the merits to the True Sovereigns of this Hall. We rely upon the assembly to recite [the prayers], etc.
On the Eve of the Year’s End: It is essential to note that as the Great Artificer operates in secret, the cycle of the year draws to a close.

All rejoice in the stability of the four seasons and prepare to inaugurate the auspiciousness of the three yang months. We respectfully assemble the great assembly and solemnly proceed to the Spirit Shrine (as before).
10. The Position for Arranging Alms Bowls (*pātra-sthāna*):

If the Prior of the Front Hall or the Rear Hall has retired, at dawn, upon hearing the signal for the minor silence (*kṣudra-śānti*), the Hall Attendant shall request that the participants partake of the medicinal broth (*yūṣa*).

After the broth is finished, they are escorted back to their respective bowl positions and perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*ch’uk-li*). This applies whether it be the Head Seat from various regions (*shǒuzuò*) or the Prior (*dùsì*).
Regarding the assignment of quarters in the West Hall: one shall serve as the head of the division.
XI. On Bells, Fish-Shaped Bells, Drums, and Wooden Clappers:

For the bells, fish-shaped bells, drums, and wooden clappers, there are regular intervals for dawn and dusk; their length, brevity, speed, and slowness must follow the prescribed commands without fail.
This is the standard for instructing people within this monastic community: to inspire trust through silence. The morning bell breaks the long night and awakens those who sleep;
the evening bell brings awareness to the dark path and dispels obscurity. When striking the mallet, the motion should be slow and the sound drawn out.

There are three rounds, each consisting of thirty-six strikes, totaling one hundred and eight. This allows for a temporary escape from the wheel of suffering and brings rest to the three miserable realms.

How sorrowful! To manifest the profound essence of the Dharma-gate and to realize the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the practitioner who strikes the bell should burn incense and prostrate, reciting the Verse of the Bell:

"May this sound of the bell transcend the Dharma-realm; May it reach all the way through the darkness of the Iron Ring Mountains. May those in the three miserable realms be freed from suffering and cease the wheel of blades;

May all sentient beings attain perfect enlightenment. After invoking the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one should then strike the bell. Its benefit is great indeed. As for the commencement of the Dharma, one should prepare the full array of offerings.
When ascending the hall for incense burning and recitation, the signal bell for sending and receiving is struck only once, without a fixed number of strikes.

As for the small bell before the Sangha Hall, it is rung to assemble the monastics of this monastery. Whenever it is rung seven times—during the times for morning and midday meals, as well as during the circumambulation and recitation on the first and fifteenth days of the month—it indicates that the abbot is entering the hall.
If it is for the opening of the period of silent meditation, then...
When sounding the cloud-board to assemble the novices, one strikes the wooden fish. The signals given by the drum vary according to the occasion:

for preaching the Dharma, there is the Dharma-drum; for tea assemblies, the tea-drum; for the turning of the Tripitaka, the Tripitaka-drum; and for opening the bath, reporting the meal, and leading the watches.
There are also drums for each [hall]. Furthermore, when there is a great general summons (*sāmānya-ājñā*) and the assembly of monks proceeds to attend, the drum is likewise struck.

These matters that constitute the established monastic community (*dharmasaṃgha*) should all be known in advance. Even if one is secluding oneself in a hermitage or a mountain cave, practicing meditation in a remote and secluded place, upon hearing the sound and turning back to listen, one should emerge from *samādhi* and compose one’s countenance;
perhaps rolling up one’s mat to don the robe—how could this be a violation of the proper time or a loss of the right occasion? For those who preside over the Dharma and wish the assembly...
Maintain strict discipline. First, ensure that the morning and evening bells and drums are clearly distinguished; thus, all matters will naturally follow their proper order.
When visitors arrive, even if they have not yet met the master, one can know his worth from this. The "One Article on the Rules for Alerting the Assembly" has already been explained in detail.

Now, the general outline is provided as follows: The *yuban* (fish-board), the great bell (*dàzhōng*), and the hall bell (*sēngtáng zhōng*) are presided over by the administrators of the storehouse and the administrative office.

The Dharma drum (*fǎgǔ*) and the tea drum (*chágǔ*) are presided over by the attendants (*shìzhě*). Regarding the aforementioned Dharma drum for ascending the hall (*shàngtáng*): it is struck three long times. For the informal discourse (*xiǎocān*), it is struck once long.

Three strikes upon entering the hall; a general announcement for the incense offering (gaoxiang) with five strikes each. As when specifically honoring a senior monk (zunsu), the assembly, or the new and old administrative officers, strike the tea drum once.
Three strikes to withdraw from the seat. If the Head Seat (shouzuo) or the West Hall (xitang) monk holds the whisk (bingfu), they borrow the tea drum and strike it long once.
The drum in front of the Kitchen Hall (kutang) is presided over by the Kitchen Office (kusī); it is used to announce meals.

Three strikes. In the hall, tea and soup are boiled and served; the assembly gathers and then withdraws from their seats. For daily meals and congee, one strikes the bell after bowing (wa-nan) upon leaving the hall.
For a great communal labor (daipuqing), strike it once for a long duration. In some places, the drum beneath the triple gate is struck to assemble the administrators and heads;
when welcoming donors at the gate, strike five times. When the assembly receives them, strike once for a long duration.
12. On the Appointment and Removal of the Chief of the Quarters:
Whenever the term of the chief of the quarters is to begin or end, after the period of Great Stillness has concluded on that day, the Rector shall light the candles in the Guest Hall.

Wait for the retiring former *liáozhǔ* (head of the quarters) to take his leave. Perform one prostration with the head touching the ground (*chùlǐ*) and escort him out. A *xíngzhě* (attendant) follows behind to invite [the new master] to the meal.
After the meal, drink tea. Next, light the lamps and proceed to the communal quarters (*zhòngliáo*). Invite the new *liáozhǔ*. Burn incense and drink medicinal soup (*tāng*).

When the soup is finished, rise; burn another stick of incense and announce: "The *liáozhǔ* has requested to retire. As the position must not remain vacant, we respectfully request that such-and-such a person be appointed as the *liáozhǔ*. Once the invitation is concluded, [proceed] before the incense burner.

Perform a prostration by touching the ground. Escort [the guest] back to the communal quarters (*sōryō*). The attendant (*gyōja*) reports this to the quarters. Strike the small board (*sappan*) inside the quarters three times.

The *vinaya-dhara* (*uinna*) enters the gate with his hands raised in greeting (*monbun*), performs a prostration by touching the ground, and then lowers his hands. The head of the quarters (*ryōshu*) raises his hands in return.

Again, a prostration by touching the ground is performed. Escort the *vinaya-dhara* out. The attendant of the Hall Office (*dōshi*) follows to invite [the guest]. After the midday meal has concluded, perform a special service for them.

Regarding tea: the attendant of the Holy Monk (Śāstr) accompanies him. If the monastery is large and the number of residents is great, those who have not yet fulfilled the ten precepts shall take turns serving as the *liáozhǔ* (cell master).
In small temples, the *xingzhě* (novice practitioner) shall perform this duty.

13. Praise for the Recitation of a Sick Monk. Having finished the praise, one says: "This morning, there is a certain bhikṣu who is ill. He seeks to release the enmity of many lifetimes and repent the transgressions of kalpas. With particular sincerity, he looks upward to strike upon the pure assembly, extolling the holy names to wash away deep calamities.

We rely upon the venerable assembly to recite: 'The Pure Dharma Body,' and so forth. The Dedication says: "We humbly pray that his single mind may be pure, his four elements light and at ease, and that his lifespan and wisdom-life may be extended. His physical form..."

The Dharma-body of the body and so forth is firm and solid. Once again, I trouble the venerable assembly with my thoughts. (In the ten directions, etc. If the illness is grave, one should offer ten recitations of the name of Amitābha Buddha.

Regarding the method for this recitation: first, after praising Amitābha Buddha, one next makes the following declaration: "Today, there is a sick bhikṣu named [Name], who, while in illness, seeks to release the enmity of many lifetimes and repent the transgressions of kalpas.

He has specially applied his sincere resolve to look up to the pure assembly and invoke the holy name, in order to wash away deep-seated calamities. We now rely upon the venerable assembly to recite: 'Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. (Recite with a long, drawn-out voice.)
Recite [the name] one hundred times. Recite the names of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva ten times each. Then, perform the dedication as follows:

(I humbly pray that, should my various conditions not yet be exhausted, I may quickly attain ease; should my life-force be difficult to prolong, may I go directly to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. [Ten Directions, Three Periods of Time... and so forth. At this time, you should gather the mind in purity and must not allow it to wander toward worldly affairs.

14. On the Contemporary Abbot’s Entry into Nirvana When the World-Honored One manifested his passing, and when the various patriarchs entered *nirvāṇa*, there were established scriptures for their encoffining and rites for their conduct that followed a proper order. Yet, whenever I observe the practices in various regions, I see that they entrust the affairs of the World-Honored One and the patriarchs to the laity.
Some say: "There is no need to follow the teachings; one should merely raise a public lamentation, and perform only a mental mourning (*xin-sang*). This, too, is...
To briefly summarize one aspect: in recent times, others have emulated and practiced this. Fearing that future generations might not hear of it, I shall set forth the general outline.
For instance, at the Twin Trees, [the Buddha] was respectfully enshrined within a golden coffin. Ānanda and the other disciples were choked with grief and filled with sorrow;
they wept until their blood flowed like *pāṭala* flowers. Śakra, Brahmā, the nāgas, and the devas wailed and leaped about in mourning, their tears falling like rain for seven days.
Kāśyapa arrived from a foreign land, regretting that he had not beheld the true likeness of the Buddha. Suddenly, the outer coffin revealed the pair of footprints.
Thereafter, by means of the Great Sovereign Samādhi, he caused the golden coffin to ascend into the great void and circumambulate the city of Kuśinagara three times.

They then proceeded to cremate [the remains]. The eight kingdoms raised armies and contended for the division of the *śarīra*, each returning with their portion to erect stupas; was this not in accord with the ritual classics?
During the Jingde era, the ministers compiled a record of the regulations of the Great Wisdom Chan Master of Baizhang, including two instances of [the master] wearing his head-cloth (*ding*).

The surplus belongings of deceased monks shall be entirely distributed and expended to provide funeral requisites. Those items for which an imperial edict was requested and granted shall be included in the Tripitaka and established as a permanent legal precedent.

When a venerable elder passes away, he is first bathed and dressed in his robes, then placed in the coffin. He is set within the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), where incense and flowers are offered as worship.
A verse of final instruction is pasted upon a plaque and hung to the left and right of the funeral altar. One is invited from a neighboring monastery to preside over the funeral rites;
alternatively, among the assembly of venerable elders, a Dharma relative (*dharmabandhu*) may be requested to preside. If no such Dharma relative is available, then...

First, request the venerable elders of the monastery; thereafter, draft the final testament to inform the officials, donors, monastic authorities, neighboring elders, dharma-heir disciples, and intimate Dharma relatives.
Request that monks write out separate items for the funeral inventory.
The funerary offerings shall remain in the abbot’s quarters for three days; after that period, the shrine is moved.
When moving the shrine-casket for the first time, invite one venerable elder to lift the spirit-seat (there is a *dharmaghoṣa* [Dharma-verse] for this).
Once the *dharmaghoṣa* has been recited, move the casket down and place it in the western chamber. Again, invite another person to lock the casket (there is a *dharmaghoṣa* for this).

Use a cloth curtain, white flowers, lamps, candles, and various offerings. The dharma-heir and junior disciples shall all remain behind the casket curtains, wearing mourning attire, and guard the casket.

In the eastern section of the Dharma Hall, red and purple curtains are hung, and a bed with a canopy, quilts, mattresses, and bedding is arranged. In front, a leaning desk is placed, upon which rest a whisk and a staff.
On the left side, a clothing rack is set up for the dharma robes; on the right side, there are a spittoon, a water basin, and items such as a clean towel.

In the center of the Dharma Hall, hang the portrait using a silk curtain. Extensively arrange lamps, candles, food, drink, and all implements for offering, exactly as prescribed in the final instructions.
Invite the presiding mourner (sang-zhu); the presiding mourner must not decline or evade the duty. When the presiding mourner arrives at the gate, strike the great bell.
The head monks and administrators shall lead the assembly to welcome them. Upon reaching the dormitory hall, they shall be settled there. After the serving of tea and soup is completed, both...
The procession leads the filial son forward; he burns incense and pays obeisance to make his request. One must prepare in advance items such as mourning garments to present to the chief mourner.
Next, a consultation is held to invite the various officiants: two stewards (pālacai), the funeral director (sangsi), the *vinaya* master, the secretary, the guest prefect, and the attendant.
If these are former associates, one invites them as officiants according to the usual protocol for requesting others. After the tea has been consumed, they rise and burn incense.

One incense stick is offered. [The participants] return to their positions and stand. They announce the request for personnel and return once more before the burner to make the formal invitation, bowing down again.

Once the appointment of officials is concluded, they serve hot soup and withdraw. Next, the head of the assembly (cāndra) and the attendant (karmadāna) are summoned; it is appropriate to assign one section of the funeral office (śmaśānādhipati).

When the attendants have finished their duties, one should first invite the *vina* (rectifier), prepare the list, and arrange the invitations for the heads of the quarters (*śirṣa*), the western hall (*paścimamaṇḍapa*), and the elders of the western class.

Regarding matters such as the various mountain temples, the administration of ritual affairs, the relocation of the shrine, or the locking of the shrine, these must be requested and assigned with equal distribution to avoid any grounds for suspicion.
The presiding mourner may only accept the small *can* (sermon) before the spirit tablet and lead the wailing;
for all other duties, they must not concurrently hold office. Furthermore, if there are traveling monks or attendants accompanying them, they must by no means be involved in these ritual functions.

Once the funeral couch and seating have been arranged, preparations are made in advance for the wailing and the sacrificial food. The bell is struck to assemble the congregation. The attendant comes forward to present the deceased’s final words;
the head seat (shouzuo) and the assembly write them down, which the presiding mourner (zhusangren) receives by drawing lots.

The head seat burns incense, and after the rector (weina) has finished reading [the text], the presiding mourner is invited to wail (accompanied by a formal discourse). Thereafter, the filial son and the assembly begin their wailing.

He weeps several times. The filial son burns incense, offers tea and soup, and presents the sacrificial offerings. The *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) proclaims the liturgy. The filial son performs prostrations before the portrait and returns to the mourning tent.
The presiding mourner burns incense and pays respects to the portrait; next, the two classes of officials burn incense and pay respects to the portrait.

The presiding mourner proceeds to the mourning tent to offer condolences to the filial son. The filial son performs three prostrations; the presiding mourner replies with one bow. Next, the administrative officers [perform the same].

The head preceptor and the assembly, having finished their condolences for the filial son, accompany the remains to partake of the medicinal broth. The two classes of officials attend before the remains morning and evening to burn incense and recite sutras at the shrine;
they pay their respects to the presiding mourner and provide offerings of vegetarian meals and gruel according to the community.
Whenever a person arrives to offer condolences, the outer *zhike* (guest master) first inquires as to their origin, their relationship to the deceased, and their social standing.
He then dispatches someone to inform the inner *zhike*, who sends mourning garments and a headcloth to the visitor. The visitor then accepts the ritual offerings for the memorial service.

The inner *zhike* leads the visitor before the portrait to burn incense and present the offerings. Next, they proceed to the spirit niche and the spirit bed, burning incense on both sides, and finally return before the portrait.

Perform prostrations. Read the memorial text; if no one is available to read it, let the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) of this temple or the *karmadāna* (administrative secretary) recite it on his behalf.

Next, offer condolences to the filial son, as well as to the administrators (*karmadāna*) and the head monks (*śreṣṭhin*). Serve tea and soup to the presiding mourner, and provide him with a mourning robe and cap;
these items are generally provided according to the specific circumstances.

1. First, express one’s own grief. At nightfall, provide offerings of tea and soup while performing recitations; these should be conducted according to the family’s means, whether abundant or modest. 2.
The presiding mourner must calculate the quantity of the deceased’s robes and alms bowl, silently dividing them into three equal portions.

One portion shall cover the expenses for the mourning attire of the ritual officials, the chanting of scriptures, and the provision of lamps and candles. One portion shall be returned to the permanent endowment (changzhu) to supplement the offerings.
Provisions for the funeral offerings shall be prepared. One portion shall be distributed to the assembly for the purpose of reading scriptures and for general expenses.

The presiding mourner (zhǔsāng) shall consult with the treasurer (zhǎngcái) to ensure that no deficiencies arise which might lead to disorder. Each day, the funeral director (sāngsī) shall prepare clean and orderly accounts.
Furthermore, one person from the Office for Managing Disciples shall be appointed in advance to provide remuneration and offerings.

First, they shall perform memorial rites at various locations. The treasurer shall clearly prepare detailed accounts; after setting aside funds for future use, any remaining items shall revert to the permanent property of the monastery.
One portion is distributed as mourning garments:
a cloth robe and headcloth for the principal mourner; a silk robe and headcloth for the administrator;
and a robe and headcloth for the head monk. The robe and headcloth [are provided] for the [other] officers.
The senior monks and internal and external attendants shall fold their head-cloths; the lay attendants near the Abbot’s quarters shall fold their head-cloths;
the hall-attendants and the assembly of practitioners shall fold their head-cloths; and the neighboring elders shall fold their waist-scarves.
Donations from donors near and far; head-dress cloths for the administrative officers; cotton shirts and towels;
cotton shirts and towels for the heads of various work gangs; and cotton towels for the fire-attendants.

The above concerns the mourning garments (*kō-e*). Whether they are present or absent, and their relative weight or importance, shall be determined by the presiding mourner, the filial son, and the officiating priests as the occasion requires.
First is the sequence of ritual services (*hōji*).
Moving the shrine; locking the shrine; hanging the portrait; raising the lamentation; offering tea; offering soup;
holding a minor *sīmān* (small *pratisaṃvid*) discourse before the spirit;
raising the shrine; hanging the portrait at the entrance; offering tea at the entrance; offering soup at the entrance; and carrying the torch.
Fold the robe, lift the bones, and place them in the stupa, returning them to the Patriarchs’ Hall.
If the remains have been kept in the shrine for many days, or if there are many people attending the rites,
one should offer tea and soup as a memorial offering every day according to the prescribed sequence.
The administrative heads, the chief officiant, the presiding mourners,
the assembly, the elders, the various manor residents and country folk,
the Dharma relatives, the patrons from the various mountains, the attendants, and the junior disciples.

The practitioner-monks and lay attendants held a small *chan* (meditation) discourse one night. On the following day, the administrative officers, together with the filial sons, invited the presiding mourner to deliver a small *chan* discourse before the spirit tablet. They submitted this request:

"Venerable Abbot, since you have already entered parinirvāṇa, we are all grieving as if we had lost our own mothers. We venture to request that you, Venerable Presiding Mourner, come at evening to deliver a small *chan* discourse before the spirit tablet. We pray most earnestly for your compassion and grant us your special permission."
After a night of recitation, the Hall Master hangs up the notice following the midday meal. When the evening bell tolls, the assembly gathers.

After the informal sermon (*hsiao-ts'an*) has concluded, the senior administrative official burns incense and offers tea, soup, and food. Once this is finished, the *vinaya* master steps forward, bows to the two classes of officials, and completes the incense offering.

The Venerable Vinaya Master turns around and addresses the assembly before the spirit tablet, saying: "Venerable Assembly, our Abbot, the Dharma Master, has already returned to True Quiescence. The community has lost its reliance; let us but contemplate impermanence and by no means be negligent.

We rely upon the Great Assembly to recite: 'The Pure Dharma Body,' etc. After the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* has been chanted, he performs the dedication, saying: "The merit from the foregoing recitations and chanting of sutras is offered for the sake of the Abbot, the Great Chan Master [Name].

We humbly pray that the *tathāgata-puṣpa* (Flower of the Tathāgata) may appear once more, spreading the springtime of the Garden of Enlightenment; and that the Sun of Wisdom may shine forever long, eternally illuminating the night of the dark alleys. We trouble the Great Assembly again to recite: 'The Ten Directions,' etc. The Guest Prefect.

Having finished chanting the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī with palms held level, the dedication is recited as follows: "By the merit of the above recitation of the sutra, we respectfully dedicate it for the Abbot, that his rank and station may be further exalted. To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time... and so forth.

Lifting the reliquary casket once, the recitation says: "The golden coffin rises of its own accord, circumambulating the great city of Kuśinagara; banners and streamers sway in the void as it proceeds to the magnificent rite of cremation [the funeral is called Nandi]. We rely upon the great assembly."
Recite the Great Name to express one's longing and devotion; may this serve to support the path to enlightenment and contemplate the Pure Dharma-body, and so forth.

First, regarding the rites for the funeral procession: they must be conducted with propriety. The large coffin should be elaborately adorned, as should the True Shrine (*zhentíng*) and the Incense Shrine (*xiāngtíng*). During the ritual services, banners and flowers should be displayed.

On the day the coffin is raised, the home temple shall provide a great vegetarian feast according to its means, and the distribution of alms (*kṣaṇadāna*) should exceed that of ordinary occasions. This is the duty of filial piety.

After the son has circumambulated the reliquary niche, the presiding mourner and those below him, the funeral procession attendants, and the assembly of the local monastery shall each hold flowers and willow branches and proceed one after another.
The officials and patrons walk on either side of the assembly, moving along together.
The nuns and the deceased’s family members follow at the rear.

First, the Platform of Nirvana. The liturgical recitation says: (On this day, there was a newly deceased Abbot; having completed his work for the sake of sentient beings, he suddenly returned to true permanence. His sacred shrine is now encircled by the city of Kuśinagara.)

On this day, the fire of one's own nature shall spontaneously consume [the body]. We rely upon the venerable assembly to assist and support the awakening spirit. *Namo* Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss—[The assembly joins in: "Amitābha Buddha. [Having recited ten times. Thus far, we have extolled the holy name.

We respectfully honor your transformative conduct. We pray that you will embody the ultimate essence of the ancestral school; that your sublime capacity remains beyond the reach of Buddhas and patriarchs as you establish a model for emulation; and that your compassionate heart continues to gather in devas and humans as you withdraw your illusory physical frame into the *samādhi* of the fire-light.

As the three libations of tea are poured and a single incense burner is lit, we receive these instructions with the highest reverence and pay homage to the assembly of sages. After the Venerable Leader (Vina) has finished reciting the *Mahākaruṇā-mantra*, he performs the dedication of merit, saying:

18. On the Anniversary of the Patriarchs’ Death:

For those who have appeared in the world to guide and transform others through the Dharma-gate, how could the anniversary of the patriarchs' death be allowed to pass in vain? At the very least, one should make offerings.

Next, the ritual prostrations and the chanting of scriptures shall be performed. One must take this deeply to heart and treat one another with mutual respect. This is conducted as for the anniversary of a Great Patriarch’s passing:

If there are offerings and monetary gifts at the time of the vegetarian feast, one should chant the sutra during the mid-feast; the ritual procedures are as before.

At the conclusion of the summer retreat (*kṣayana*), fearing that the heads and administrative officers (*śrāmaṇera-karmadāna*) might be preoccupied with social affairs—such as attending the morning assembly after the congee meal—the community shall rest for half a month.

May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm universally aspire to manifest their own innate wisdom and turn the Great Dharma Wheel within every atom of the lands. When the preaching of the Dharma is concluded, it is said: "Descend from the seat. Together, proceed to the Great Buddha Hall to perform prostrations and recite scriptures.

The First Month Division. On the first day: after the morning gruel, the assembly takes their seats and tea is served. Furthermore, the two classes of officials from the single quarters are invited to the Abbot’s quarters for tea, following the usual protocol.

After descending from the hall, the sutras are chanted in the Dharma Hall to offer prayers for the Emperor. After a short while, the Abbot ascends the seat. The formal greetings at the foot of the Dharma seat are the same as those for the Winter Solstice;

[Having realized the patience of non-arising,] next, the seat is spread and it is said: "This morning, we reverently encounter the Great Monk, our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Tathāgata, on the occasion of his parinirvāṇa. To transcend the mundane and leave the secular world, one dons the shaven head and the square-cut robe; generally, having experienced the monastic communities (sōlin), one must thoroughly understand their regulations.

Their conduct was unacquainted with the proper laws, and their movements did not accord with the Vinaya rules. Although they were virtuous friends and good companions, how could they have been willing to apply the deep needle and the piercing probe?
Habitual practice had become a corruption, and reform was difficult; this caused the monastic groves to fall into desolation and further led people's minds to grow indolent.
Having repeatedly observed these common faults before our very eyes, I have therefore compiled the established models of Baizhang.
Examine the beginning and seek the end; from morning until evening, strive to avoid failure at every turn.

You must practice each and every instruction with precision before you dare claim to have investigated yourself, clarified the mind, understood life, and mastered death. The worldly dharma is itself the supramundane dharma.
This may be passed on by those who have traveled the path to those who have not yet traveled it, so that they may not fail the purpose of their renunciation of household life. Furthermore—
To repay the kindness and virtue of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, I have prepared the following instructions for entering the assembly.
As for the method of sleeping and rising: one must not sleep before others nor rise after them.

One should rise quietly before the five o'clock bell has even sounded, lifting the body first and placing the pillow behind the feet; it should not yet be folded, lest its sound startle the neighbors.
Single-mindedly, rouse your spirit. Wrap yourself in the bedding, sit upright and remain motionless; do not fan the air, lest it cause others to become distracted.

When you feel fatigue approaching, push the bedding back toward your feet, turn around, and take the handkerchief to descend from the bed. Place the handkerchief over your left hand and recite this verse:

"From the morning dawn until evening, all sentient beings have mutually accommodated one another. If I should lose my life beneath these feet, I vow that you shall immediately be reborn in the Pure Land. [Recite lightly.]

Lift the curtain with your hand and exit through the rear section; do not wear slippers, and do not cough or make any noise. As the ancients said: "When lifting the curtain, one must keep the hand trailing behind;
when exiting the hall, take care not to drag your sandals. Take the washbasin with a light hand and wash your face; the water should not be used in excess.
When using tooth-cleaning powder, take it with the right hand and apply it to the left side of the mouth; then take it with the left hand and apply it to the right side.

One must not apply it again with both hands simultaneously, for fear of passing on dental disease or bad breath to others. When rinsing and spitting out the water, one must bend the head and guide the water down with the hand;
one must not spit while keeping the waist straight, lest the water splash into the neighbor's bucket. One must not wash one's head. There are four items [to observe].
This is disadvantageous to both oneself and others: first, it defiles the bucket; second, it defiles the hand-towel—these are disadvantages to others. Third, it causes the hair to wither;
fourth, it damages the eyes—these are disadvantages to oneself. One must not make sounds within the nostrils, nor should one vomit at a loud voice.
The ancients said: Washing the face at the fifth watch is fundamentally for the purpose of spiritual cultivation. If one makes sounds while spitting, it disturbs the hall and annoys the assembly.
Having finished wiping the face, one returns to the hall; if staying in the upper section, the left foot enters first, and if in the lower section, the right foot enters first.

Returning to one’s bedding position, when about to lie down on the mat, one should fold it in half. Once seated, if changing into the *zhidu* (straight robe), one must cover the body with the new garment.

One must not expose the white undergarment. One must not fan the wind. If one wishes to burn incense and prostrate in the hall, it is appropriate to take the *kāṣāya* secretly outside the rear gate before the bell has sounded and put it on there.
When leaving one’s seat at ordinary times, one should don the *kāṣāya*, join the palms above the head, and recite this verse:
“Excellent is this robe of liberation; Its merit is formless, yet derived from cloth. I now receive it upon my head; May I wear it in every lifetime. After folding the *kāṣāya*, first...
When folding the hands, one should later unfasten the ring. One must not hold the *kāṣāya* with the mouth, nor hook the *kāṣāya* with the chin.

Once the folds are finished, one should also perform a formal greeting (*praṇāma*) before departing. When performing prostrations in the hall, one must not occupy the center, thereby obstructing the arrival of the abbot.
One must not chant the Buddha’s name aloud, nor pass by the heads of those who are prostrating. One must...
Go to the empty space behind the hall. At the striking of the bell at the fifth watch, when the abbot and the head seat are seated in the hall, one must not enter or exit through the front gate.
Once the small *jing* (bell) has been struck (and the wooden clapper has ceased), one may then fold the bedding and adjust the pillow. As for the method of folding the bedding:
first find the two corners and, with the hands, straighten them forward. First fold one half, then fold the half in front of the body. Do not...
If you must occupy an adjacent unit, you must not shake it or make noise. You must not fan yourself with a cloth.

Alternatively, you may go to the communal quarters to take medicine or to the tea hall for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Upon returning, place your bowl in its designated position, turning your upper shoulder in sequence (meaning the left shoulder).
If entering through the front gate, enter from the southern side; do not walk along the northern side or the center, for these areas are revered.

When the abbot is presiding, if the wooden fish is struck, one must not enter the hall. Alternatively, the attendant may be ordered to take the bowl and sit outside the hall, or return it to the communal quarters.
Once the striking is finished and one enters the hall, one must return to one’s place for the bowl, bowing with head lowered to pay respects to the senior, middle, and junior seats.
If one has already taken one’s seat when a superior, middle, or inferior-ranking elder approaches, one must join the palms. As the ancients said:

"If one does not show respect to superior, middle, or inferior-ranking elders, there is no difference between this and a gathering of Brahmins. Upon hearing the long board (changban) strike, one sets down the bowl, straightens the body to stand upright, and then turns around.
This too must be done with the shoulder facing toward the superior; only after joining the palms may one take up the bowl. With one hand, one releases the hook, while the left hand holds it.
Turn the body to face forward. Squat down to place the bowl away, taking care not to strike others with the waist or back.

When the bell rings before the hall, descend from the platform to perform a greeting (*wenshen*) to welcome the abbot; do not swing your arms left and right. When descending from the platform, you must step forward to perform a greeting;
do not allow the *kāṣāya* to drape over the edge of the platform. Furthermore, when ascending the platform, one must do so low and carefully, without dropping the body abruptly.

Take the bowl and place it before the seat. Upon hearing the sound of the mallet, recite the verse of mindfulness: "The Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, Attained enlightenment in Magadha, Taught the Dharma in Vārāṇasī, And entered parinirvāṇa in Kuśinagara.

The method for unfolding the bowl is as follows: First, join the palms and recite the verse: "This vessel of the Tathāgata, I now unfold; May I, together with all beings, Be equal in the emptiness and stillness of the three wheels.
Thereafter, remove the cloth wrapper. Unfold the clean towel and drape it over the knees. Fold the wrapper into a triangle and ensure that no part of it protrudes.

Regarding the single outer cloth: first, unfold the bowl-cloth. With the left hand palm up, take the bowl and place it upon the cloth. Using the thumbs of both hands, pick up the rim of the bowl and unfold it from the bottom upward in sequence;
do not let it clatter or make noise. Furthermore, protect the fourth and fifth fingers (the ring and little fingers) as they are considered "defiled" fingers and must not be used.
Fold the bowl-cloth to make it small, and place the bag for the spoon and chopsticks near the body, laid horizontally.
When entering [the hall], the spoon is placed first; when leaving, the chopsticks are placed first. The part of the handle held in the hand is the "clean end.
Pointing toward the shoulder, the bowl-brush is placed within the seam of the second lid, protruding about half an inch, to hold raw rice.

One must not use the tips of the spoon or chopsticks to take out the raw rice, nor should more than seven grains be taken. Taking too little is considered stingy eating. (In all cases of receiving food, one uses the "taking-out" method; however, if not receiving food, one must not reach directly into the bucket or ladle.)
(When scooping rice for the birth ceremony), the *vinaya-dhara* recites the Buddha’s name. With palms joined, the fingers must not be uneven; they must be held at the chest, at the proper height.
One must not rest the hands against the edge of the mouth. An ancient saying goes: "Palms joined unevenly, not level with the chest;
hands crossed and thrust into the nose; dragging sandals and lifting the curtain without courtesy; making gurgling sounds and releasing gas while boasting of one's prowess. Both hands...

Holding the alms bowl to receive food, one should contemplate with the verse: "When receiving food, I vow that all sentient beings shall take the joy of dhyāna as their sustenance and be filled with the delight of the Dharma. Whether the portion be much or little.

Then, with the right hand, one begins and ends [the meal]. Upon hearing the signal for universal eating (*piānshí*), one observes the upper and lower shoulders and faces the food with the front of the face.
One must not face the food directly; rather, one gestures toward both sides with the hands. Having finished the gesture, one performs the five reflections (*wuguàn*), contemplating as follows:

(1) Calculating the amount of labor expended and measuring the distance from whence it came; (2) Reflecting upon one’s own virtue and conduct to determine whether one is worthy of this offering; (3) Guarding the mind against transgressions, making it the primary aim to remain free from greed and other afflictions; (4) Regarding the food as wholesome medicine intended to treat the emaciation of the physical body; (5) Accepting it for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path.

Regarding this food, the verse for generating mindfulness says: "O assembly of spirits and deities, I now bestow upon you this offering. This food pervades the ten directions; may all spirits and deities partake together. Such is the method for consuming the food.
One must not bring the mouth toward the food, nor bring the food toward the mouth. When picking up or setting down the bowl, as well as the spoon and chopsticks, one must not make any sound.
One must not cough, nor pinch the nose or sneeze. If one should happen to sneeze, one should cover the nose with the sleeve of one's robe.
One must not scratch the head, for fear that wind-blown dandruff might fall into the bowls of neighboring seats. One must not pick at the teeth with the hand.
One must not chew food or slurp soup while making noise. One must not pick at the center of the bowl. One must not take large mouthfuls.
One must not open one's mouth to wait for food. One must not let food fall and scatter. One must not eat by scattering grains with the hand.

If there are vegetable scraps, they should be placed behind the bowl in a concealed spot. One must not fan one’s neighbor with the wind; if one is fanning oneself, one should do so in such a way that it does not disturb others.
He immediately informed the *karmadāna* and sat outside the hall. He must not rest his hand upon his knee. He should receive food according to his portion and must not request more.
He must not use his head-bowl (*thōp*) to hold wet food, nor must he skim the broth from within the head-bowl.
Rinse the rice bowl. You must not pick up vegetable heads from the bowl and eat them with the rice. When eating, you must observe those above and below your shoulders;
do not eat too slowly. Until you have been invited to take more, do not scrub the bowl. Do not make a sound by sucking on the bowl-brush.
If food has not yet arrived, do not give rise to vexation. As the ancients said: "Foolishly looking around, one gives rise to grief and anger; mindful of the food, one swallows saliva."
Coughing and frequent spitting, he stuffs his mouth full of gruel and soup; opening the cloth and spreading out the bowl, his clatter reaches all the neighbors.
When washing the bowl, he uses the head-bowl to hold water and washes the bowls one by one, but not inside the head-bowl; he then washes the spoons, chopsticks, and the bowls together.
One should still keep the fourth and fifth fingers bent. One must not make noise while washing or rinsing the mouth.
One must not spit water into the bowl. One must not first wash the bowl with hot water. Before the water has been drained, one must not first put away the knee-cloth (*jī-mo*).

One must not wipe sweat with the knee-cloth. One must not pour leftover water onto the ground. When reciting the verse for draining the water, one should contemplate as follows: "This bowl of mine..."

Water: Like the nectar of the heavens, I offer it to the assembly of spirits and deities, so that all may be fully satisfied. *Oṃ māhura se svāhā*. To collect the bowls: With both hands, join the thumbs together and enter [the bowls] in sequence.

Once finished, join the palms. Contemplate the verse for the conclusion of the meal: "Having finished eating, physical strength and radiance are restored; His majestic power shakes the ten directions, a hero of the three periods of time.

He does not dwell on causes or turn toward fruits; All sentient beings attain supernatural powers. When the board sounds in front of the quarters, return to the quarters to inquire after one’s fellows, but do not return to your own seat.

To avoid showing disrespect to the assembly, enter the hall and take your place according to the rules of the Sangha hall. Stand still and wait until the *liáozhǔ* (hall master) has finished burning incense;

then, exchange greetings with those above and below you. If there is tea, take your seat. Do not let your robes hang down; do not huddle together laughing or talking; do not bow to others with only one hand;
and do not conceal tea dregs in your sleeves. As the ancients said: "When ascending the platform for a formal sitting, one must remain composed."
When the robe is worn with the hem hanging down, one may greet others with a single hand; what is the principle behind this?
One must not privately store tea dregs, as this invites derision from onlookers. At all times, practitioners at neighboring desks must strictly avoid whispering to one another.

After tea, whether reading a sutra or walking in the quarters, one must not spread the scroll out long (meaning both sides simultaneously), nor rest the hands upon the scroll. While walking in the hall, one must not let the sash hang down and must not make noise.

One must not lean one's back against the headboard while reading scriptures. An ancient said: "To chant aloud and disturb the crowd, or to lean one's back against the headboard and show contempt for the assembly, is improper.
One must leave the quarters in advance; do not wait until the sitting board is struck. If you are late, you must withdraw immediately.
According to ancient custom, one wears the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*). Taking a clean cloth, drape it over the left arm, untie the sash, and fasten it to the bamboo staff.
Remove the hanging loops from the *jīzhí dùn* (straight-cut robe) and arrange them neatly; secure them with the hand and further tie a handkerchief as a marker. One must not laugh or speak.
One must not urge others from outside. Holding water in the right hand, one enters the latrine and changes shoes; they must not be placed unevenly. The clean bucket is set down in front.
One snaps the fingers three times to startle away the dung-eating spirits. One should squat with the body upright, without straining or making noise.
One must not spit or sneeze, nor converse with others through the wall. As the ancients said: "The door latch should be handled lightly."
Snap your fingers. When people are crowded together, refrain from making noise. When entering the latrine, use a wooden tally to distinguish between the defiled and the clean areas.

Upon exiting, remove your shoes, taking care not to leave them scattered haphazardly. Do not pour water onto both sides [of the vessel]. Wash with the left hand, protecting the thumb and the second finger.
One must not use too many counting sticks (*śalākā*). As the ancients said: "Use little bathing water; refrain from picking up counting sticks.
Those who have finished using them should wash them with water and place them in an empty spot by the latrine. If there are many people, it will obstruct the assembly;

they should not be kept for long. Return the clean bucket to its original place. With dry hands, put on the undergarment and enter the trousers. With dry hands, open the door, and with the right hand, lift the bucket.
When exiting, do not grasp the door leaf or the door frame with wet hands. First, use the right hand to lift the ashes, and afterwards lift the soil.
Do not use wet hands to grasp the ashes or soil, nor should you spit while mixing mud. Wash your hands first, and only then use soap nuts (*gaojiao*).
Wash down to the level of the elbows, reciting the *vārī-mantroccāraṇa* (toilet mantra) for each instance. Use water to rinse and cleanse the mouth.

According to the Vinaya, one must likewise wash clean after even minor urination, and then chew a willow branch (*dantakāṣṭha*). Return to the hall to practice seated meditation; until the fire-board has sounded, one must not return to the quarters early.
One must not wash clothes before the midday meal, before the morning gruel, before the midday meal, or after the evening session. One must not open chests or cabinets except in cases of urgency;
in such instances, inform the administrative officers, the head of the quarters within the monastery, or the attendant of the Sacred Monk in the Sangha Hall. After the meal has concluded:
One must not gather in groups within the Sangha hall to converse. One must not read sutras or scrolls while inside the Sangha hall.

One must not walk directly through the central aisle between the upper and lower sections of the hall. One must not pass coins through the mats. One must not sit with one’s feet dangling in front of the bed;

a space of one chi (one foot) in front of the bed is designated as the "three-purity zone," where: first, the alms bowl is placed; second, the *kāṣāya* is laid down; and third, [the sitting mat is arranged].

One must not walk upon the bed in the direction one’s head is pointing. One must not kneel on the knees to open a chest or cabinet. One must not step onto the edge of the bed with one’s feet to descend to the ground.
When wearing straw sandals and the five-strip robe while traveling the mountains, one must not perform *caṅkrama* (walking meditation) in the Buddha Hall or the Dharma Hall. As the ancients said:
"To enter the latrine with bared shoulders, to travel the mountains in straw sandals, and never to tread upon the Dharma Hall"—one must yield to the elders and must not go about barefoot.
When wearing monastic sandals, one must not walk with hands clasped together while discussing the right and wrong of worldly conventions. An ancient said:

"Having bid farewell to both parents and abandoned one's own teacher, one seeks out a spiritual friend—what does one intend to do? Never having spoken of the matters of the Zen school, with white hair and no achievement, on whom does the fault rest?
One must not lean against the balustrades in the hall, nor run about in wild abandon. An ancient said: "To walk..."
One must walk with slow, measured steps, practicing the majestic deportment of Aśvajit; one’s speech should be in a low voice, following the model of Upāli.
One must not wander idly through the Buddha Hall. As the ancients said: "If there is no business, do not ascend the Buddha Hall; do not casually enter within the stupa.
If one does not sweep the floor or add scented water, even the merit of the sands of the Ganges will eventually be exhausted. After the midday meal, wash one's robes.

Regarding the wearing of robes: one must not expose the chest. One must not pour hot water from the pitcher onto the clothes. Once finished using the bamboo pole, the iron brazier, or other implements, they must be returned to their original places.
When the foot-washing board rings, one must not scramble for the foot-tub. If one has sores or scabies, one should wash them last.
Alternatively, one may wash in a bucket in a secluded place to avoid disturbing the minds of the assembly. Do not wait for the striking of the *zazen* board;
proceed in order to the hall to sit in meditation. When the session is dismissed (*fangcan*), fold the meditation mat halfway.

When the board sounds before the head seat’s quarters (*shouzuo liao*), turn immediately toward the outside and must attend the assembly at once. After the board has sounded, one must neither enter the hall nor remain outside the hall.
Upon rising, the Abbot and the Head Seat leave the hall, open their mats, descend from their beds, and perform a formal greeting.

They return to their quarters for their medicinal meal, where each takes their place at the designated seat. One must not rise before others to serve food, nor call out loudly to request porridge, rice, salt, vinegar, or similar items.
When the meal is finished, one leaves the quarters; however, one must not exit through the main gate, enter a small auxiliary hall, or return to the Sangha Hall with one’s upper garment bared.
Walk along the corridors; do not wait for the striking of the wooden board to leave the quarters. When the evening bell tolls, one should immediately join the palms and recite the verse:

*Hearing the sound of the bell, afflictions grow light;* *Wisdom increases, and Bodhi arises.* *Leaving the hells, emerging from the fiery pit,* *I vow to attain Buddhahood and deliver all sentient beings.* One must first return to one’s own cell and practice seated meditation.
One must not scratch one's head on the bed, nor fiddle with prayer beads on the bed so that they make noise, nor converse with those in neighboring cells. Neighboring...
If one is alone, one should use kind words to guide and encourage others, never giving rise to feelings of resentment or aversion.

Before the bell has been struck, one must not enter or exit through the front gate. One may open it only when the pillow-bell sounds and the fire-bell has passed its time. When burning incense and prostrating, one must wait until it is deeper in the night.
If the assembly has not yet slept, one must not sleep first; if the assembly has not yet risen, one must be the first to rise.

When rising, do not disturb your neighbors in their quarters. When sleeping, you must lie on your right side; do not lie on your back, for to lie on one's back is the sleep of a corpse, and to lie face down is the sleep of a lecher;

both result in many evil dreams. Wrap the *kāṣāya* in a cloth and place it before your pillow. Nowadays, many people place it behind their feet, which is inconvenient according to the principles of the Dharma.
If you encounter an occasion for bathing, carry your bathing requisites in your right hand and enter within the threshold of the lower-ranking quarters.
Inquire after their well-being. Return to an empty space. Having finished bowing to those on your left and right, first hang the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) upon the bamboo rack.
Unfold the bathing cloak (*snāna-saṃkakṣikā*), take it out, and place it aside. Remove your upper garment; however, do not yet discard the *zhiduo* (straight-cut robe).

First, take off the lower skirt and garments, wrap your body with the foot-cloth (*pādavastra*), and only then fasten the bathing skirt (*snāna-śāṭī*). Roll up the undergarments (*kaṭhina*) and trousers (*kholi*) and place them inside the bathing cloak.
In sequence, one should remove the *zhidu* (outer robe) and place it together with the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) in one location. Take a hand-towel and tie it to the bamboo rack;

if there is no hand-towel, tie it with a cord. As the ancients said: "When the sound of the three-fold drum resounds and one enters the hall, one must distinguish between the 'defiled' and 'pure' garments by removing the upper robes and placing them aside.
Then, remove the remaining robes, fold them into a bundle, and lay them down with the opening facing inward. One must not enter the bath barefoot. One must...
When putting on sandals, scoop water in the empty space of the lower section; do not occupy the seats of the elders or senior monks (referring to the upper section).
Do not splash hot water or liquid onto the bodies of others. Do not use the bucket to soak your feet on the floor.
Do not relieve yourself or wash private parts within the bathhouse. Do not prop your feet up on the bucket. Do not laugh or speak. Do not...
One may scrub one's feet on the edge of the tub, but must not scoop out water, nor rise from the seat to pour water over the body from a bucket.
If others are present before or behind, one must shield them. One's foot-cloth must not leave the body.

If there are those who have foot-cloths but do not enter the tub, one must not use an excessive amount of bathing water for them. If one has sores, or is washing a burn, or applying ointment for scabies, it is appropriate to enter the tub last.
When bathing, one must not cut in ahead of others. One must not use the communal hand-towel to wipe the head or face;
the communal hand-towel is for use after dressing, once the hands have been washed, to wrap around the body. Upon leaving the bath, one bows to those on the left and right.
First, put on the upper garment and the *zhidu* (straight robe) to cover oneself completely, then put on the lower garments and remove the bathing skirt. Fold the bathing skirt using the foot-cloth.
Inside, fearing that the bath mat may become damp, carry the hand towel in your left hand. You must not drape a wet foot-cloth over your hands;

instead, bow to those on your left and right and exit. Observe the name of the donor who has provided the bath, and recite sūtras and dhāraṇīs at will before performing the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).

In cold months, when warming yourself by the fire, first sit upon the hearth, then turn your body and enter the fire-pit. After paying your respects, you may sit down; in some places, one removes one's shoes.
When outside [the hall], one must not play with the incense spoon or fire tongs. One must not stir up the flying embers and ashes.
One must not huddle together to talk. One must not roast snacks or other items. One must not warm shoes to remove their odor, nor dry socks or clothes over the fire.
One must not pull up one’s *zhiduo* robe to expose the hem of the trousers. One must not spit, nor cast dirt or grease into the fire. As...
The daily events previously compiled herein— the deportment within the assembly, ascending the hall, entering the room,
giving informal sermons (*xiao-can*), chanting scriptures, reciting mantras, inspecting the quarters, resolving disputes, attending to visitors, packing one's bags and donning the hat,
conducting funeral rites, and the auctioning of robes— these minute rules of conduct are already fully recorded in the *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity). I respectfully [refer you to them].
Each monastery has its own explicit regulations; there is no need to present them here again, as it would merely result in redundant speech.

It has been ten years since I transmitted this edition. One day, while I was reading through it, someone said: "It seems you have..."
I have intended to compile the rituals of the monastic community into a formal work. However, as the ages decline and customs shift, all things are swept away by change;
though my resolve was diligent, what benefit could it possibly bring? I replied: "Not so. How could the canons of a hundred generations be altered by the trends of a single era?
The Yin dynasty followed the Xia, and the Zhou followed the Yin; the points of reduction and addition are clearly discernible therein. If..."
Some may drift away and forget their way back; this book shall serve as a lid for the jars [of ignorance]. Thus, the prediction of our Buddha has been proven true, and I can do nothing about it.
On the fifth day after the conclusion of the retreat in the Jia-shen year of the Zhizhen era, Wei Mian wrote this again at the Duiyun Liao hermitage on Beishan.
The Head Seat of Pingyan has published these new regulations based on the old woodblocks, thereby guiding and uplifting future students;

what service could be greater than this? Yet, when ritual is corrupted, the Dharma falls into ruin; when the Dharma is ruined, ritual perishes. These two are like hooks and chains, or linked rings, which must not be severed;
their connection is of the utmost importance. To courageously publish these woodblocks is to desire the eternal preservation of the Great Dharma and the maintenance of ritual propriety.
Yongjia arrived at Caoxi, circumambulated the meditation seat three times, shook his mendicant’s staff, and stood there. May it be called a breach of etiquette?
May it be called a lack of the Dharma? Let those who observe this not be negligent. Written in the auspicious month of the Gui-si year of the Zhiyuan era by Fuxin Yuji (Banhui) of Jingci Monastery.
